Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume One.
Compiled by the disciples Huiqi and others. Recorded Sayings of Yunju:

When the Master entered the monastery, he pointed to the mountain gate and said: "The great gates are fully opened; the true command is completely upheld. [Disciples] rush like water and flock like clouds. Gold... [text fragment].
Chongyu Ying, leaning against his seat, said:
"From the ancient masters of old down to the present, they have been prattling on about this and that here, deceiving the barbarians and hoodwinking the Han people.
Now that the new Elder has arrived, they have all lost their edge and are left speechless. He picked up his staff and said: "A vast marsh hides the mountains; the principle—"
He was able to subdue the leopard. Zhuo leaned on his staff and held up the documents.
The entrustment at Vulture Peak is verified this very day. The Buddha-dharma pervades the world; the Imperial Grace is inexhaustible.
Ascending the seat. After offering incense, the questions and answers are not recorded. The Master then said: "The Way is before your eyes; yet what is before your eyes is not the Way.
Those who are deluded are deluded by themselves; those who awaken awaken by themselves. It admits of no deliberation and cannot be reached through verbal explanations.

If you can simply be vast and forget all conditions, then naturally it will be revealed at every touch. Even if you cite ancient and modern examples, or speak of the profound and the wondrous, you may be clever..."

Displaying clever wit and eloquence, he greatly revitalized his family tradition. I say that all of this is merely inverted, deluded imagination. From Buddha to Buddha there is the passing of the hand; from patriarch to patriarch there is the transmission.
Viewed with the correct eye, it is still merely receiving echoes by grasping at empty air. Suddenly picking up his staff, he called to the assembly, saying:
"Today, Yunju has no choice but to create yet another failure. Thirty years hence, it will not..."

To avoid being scrutinized by others, [Zhaozhou] held up his staff and said: "The momentum of a thousand peaks ceases at the foot of the mountain; the sound of ten thousand streams vanishes upon reaching the sea.
He then revealed the site for building the monastery and addressed the assembly: "Yesterday we cleared the wasteland; I ask you all to clear away the thorns and remove the tiles."
Gravel. The original foundation has already been clearly revealed; there is only the central tree that no one has been able to uproot.
Today, this mountain monk cannot help but employ another expedient means: with a sharp blade, I prune away all the profuse branches and leaves;
with a blunt hoe, I deeply dig out the crooked and inverted roots. The work upon the solid ground becomes a single expanse; the pickaxe used for dwelling in the mountains leaves no trace at all.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Great Master Yunmen, who said: "On level ground there are countless dead people;
those who can emerge from the thorny forest are true adepts. At that time, a monk said, "If that is so, then the Head Seat in the hall has a point of excellence.
Yunmen said, "Sulū sulū. The Master said: "Yunmen spoke thus, but Yunju would not have it this way. On level ground, there are living people."
"Countless! To enter the thorn forest is to be a true adept. Suddenly, if someone comes forward to speak of the long and the short, I take up my staff and strike them across the back.
Why? Water flows to what is moist; fire seeks what is dry. Calamity and fortune have no gate; it is only man who summons them himself."
Whenever the Master saw a monk, he would invariably ask: "I have recently received an official document; my duty is to interrogate you, Venerable. The monk would say, "I am no spy.
The Master would reply, "Even so, you must first undergo examination. The monk would say, "Master, do not abuse your power to oppress others.
The Master would extend his hands and say, "Bring me your credentials! If the monk hesitated, the Master would strike him with his palm. Another monk said:
"I have long heard that the Master possesses such a vital pivot. The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have suffered a loss.
The one who treasures the fire is the master; that which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. The scriptures of the Three Vehicles are entirely devoid of true meaning."
"If I call it fire, it will burn you to death; if I do not call it fire, it will freeze you to death.
A monk asked the Master, "I have heard that the Master possesses the 'mechanism of adjustment' (*dianti-jī*).

Is this true? The Master stared intently at him and said, "Are you coming forward to confess? The monk said, "The student has already overturned the meditation seat! The Master said, "Where are you from?"
A person asked, "Monk, look up with wide-open eyes! The Master said, "This is a spirit that clings to grass and perches upon wood.
On the occasion of the *Lotus Sūtra* assembly, he ascended the hall and said: "For a long time I have kept this essential teaching in silence, not wishing to speak of it hastily.
Now I shall speak of it; each of you should listen well. After a long pause, he said: "I do not dare to treat you lightly; you are all destined to become Buddhas."
Addressing the assembly: Those who act as patriarchal masters are compelled by necessity to offer a word or a phrase;

it is none other than for the sake of students—to extract nails and pull out wedges, to untangle adhesions and remove fetters. It is like a skilled dancer with the Great Sword (Ta’a): naturally, they do not injure their own hands.
In recent times, those who occupy the seat of the master and instruct disciples merely memorize texts and adorn their speech with flowery rhetoric to boast before others.
Come! You increase your evil habits and remain ignorant of the path from which you yourself emerged. It is like wearing tattered rags while walking through a thicket of thorns;
one cannot move with ease. Thus, the school of direct pointing of Shaolin has fallen to the ground here—this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.
Those of you who travel the path like the sea must each carry your own eyes; do not let yourselves fall into the nets of others, from which you will be unable to emerge.
As the ancients said: "Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.

According to my own view, even if you were to suddenly forget all such understanding, you would still be a person outside the gate. Reaching this point, you must be able to distinguish between the black and the white. Take care.
One day the Master asked a newly arrived monk, "In this place of mine, tigers and wolves block the road and thorns reach the heavens.
What urgent business brings you here, O Guest? The monk replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master said, "I do not ask about the phrase for entering the gate; tell me, where did you get those straw sandals beneath your feet? As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout.
He asked again, "Where did you come from yesterday? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. The Master said, "There is no need for further examination.
Once, while the Master was clearing weeds, a monk asked him, "When will this patch of ground be cleared until it is perfectly clean?
The Master raised his hoe and said, "Do not call this a hoe. I wonder, Elder, what would you call it? The monk was speechless.
[The Master] spoke. He threw down his hoe and said, "When will this field ever be cleared?

On the day of the summer retreat's conclusion, he ascended the hall. Today is precisely the day when the sacred regulations are fulfilled. In the monasteries of all quarters, they speak of Chan and speak of the Way.
"What a commotion! Here with me, it is solitary and towering. Even if there were Buddha-dharma, who would have eyes enough to look upon it?
He struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the student’s own self? The Master said, "Who taught you to ask such a question? The monk bowed.
The Master then said, "When one does not understand the Way upon seeing it before one's eyes, how can one know the path when setting foot upon it?
When the ancients spoke thus, it was much like laboring without merit. As for my own view, I wish for everyone to know it together. He then suddenly picked up [the whisk].
[The Master] leans on his staff, taps it once, and says: "Once the snow has melted away, spring will naturally arrive.
He then descends from the seat. One day, two monks requested instruction; the Master posed this question: "The entire great earth is one's own self."
"Where do you place your eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind? The monk remained silent. He asked a second monk:
"The peak of Mount Sumeru has smashed your skull; why do you not perceive the pain? This monk also remained silent.
The Master turned to his attendant and said, "Take note of these two turning phrases."

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Chan Master Xiangyan Sheng, who said in his ascent to the hall: "Guangjiao has a barrier for testing people, a pivot for cutting off people, and a phrase for enlivening people.
Is there anyone who can speak it? If you cannot speak it, you have brought your entire life to naught. The Master said:
At Yunju, there is no barrier for testing people, no mechanism for cutting them off, and no phrase for bringing them to life.

Is there anyone who can say it? If you cannot say it, you fail this mountain monk. Looking back at his attendant, he said, "Tell me now: was it the ancients' way that is right, or is it this old monk's way?
The attendant was speechless. The Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night in a dream, I recounted a kōan, and three people in the assembly attained realization.
When dawn broke, I tried to recount it to the great assembly, but I had forgotten it all at once. Let me wait while the old monk thinks on it further.
After a long silence, he said: "All of you, come here and listen to my dream. What reason is there for you to do so? He then struck them with his staff.
Having dispersed them at once, he ascended the hall and said:
"The Confucian books say, 'The common people use it daily yet do not know it. The Buddhist scriptures say, 'Sentient beings use it daily yet do not realize it.
I, this mountain monk, say: to know it is idle; to perceive it is delusion. These words—"
This suppresses the ancients; you must have your own eyes alive before you can succeed. (He strikes the whisk.
A thousand rivers, a thousand moons; ten thousand miles, no clouds, ten thousand miles of sky.
A monk asked the Master, “What is the place where you, the Master, truly benefit people? The Master said, “When have I ever spoken to you in empty words?
The monk said, “A master of the true lineage naturally possesses this. The Master took up his staff, struck him once, and said, “You plunderer of emptiness!
If I do not strike you now, when would I wait to do so?”
Ascending the hall, he said: "Chan cannot be investigated; the Way cannot be learned. To learn the Way and investigate Chan is to bind oneself without a rope.
A golden-maned lion exerts its full majesty; a praiseworthy qilin has but a single horn. After all, how is it?
On the wall of Zhaozhou’s Guanyin Hall hangs a gourd; sometimes the wind blows, and it rattles, *li-lo li-lo*."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it is born only by relying on conditions. When a guest comes, you must look upon them; when a thief comes, you must strike him.
Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, the Way transcends ordinary sentiment. How will you meet with him? What follows is a long discourse, which I leave for another day."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Clouds drift in layers, waters murmur; raising one's eyes, a thousand mountains and ten thousand more. The mountain countenances are silent and still; birds warble their notes.
Before the gate, the ancient path is as level as a whetstone; it does not travel with those of this age.
He struck his whisk and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "All sentient beings are turned by things. If one can turn things, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
All you practitioners of Chan, you are men; do not allow yourselves to be deceived. Now, what is it that is turned? And what is it that turns?
Śākyamuni Buddha deserves twenty blows of the staff. Nevertheless, it is well to let him go. The sword follows the wind."
Wandering through transformation, do not record the marks of chiseling on the boat.
When the Master of Transformation returns to the hall, the Chan disciples who have been guided back from Linchuan enter the gate with a smile that unfurls their brows.
Breaking through a speck of dust, they bring forth a great sutra scroll; drums are beaten and bells struck to inform the assembly. At this very moment, tell me, what is the merit?
Where do they return? Last night, spring returned beyond the void of kalpas; the fragrant blossoms of awakening opened upon branches that never sprouted.
*Incense Offering for the Anniversary of the Patriarch’s Death:* When he came, his two front teeth were missing; when he departed, he left behind a single sandal.
This old barbarian monk was reckless beyond compare. He then called out: "Is there a patriarch here? The old monk [the host] met him face-to-face with him.
Just so. Placing incense in the burner, he says: "Do not take offense at my lack of refinement. I humbly pray that you will all take care.
On account of the snow, he ascends the hall: "The great earth is covered in vast snow; The mountains are deep, their cold exceeding the usual.
No one reaches here with severed arms; Even facing the wall is without cause. Tell me, monks: is it the Patriarch who is without cause, or is it this mountain monk? He picks up his staff.
He threw down [the whisk] and said, "Groundless! Groundless!

On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and said: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the Sovereign attains the One and brings about universal peace.
When a patch-robed monk attains the One, even a drop of water freezes into ice. He took up his staff and said, "As for this very staff, when it attains the One—"
"How so? [The Master] directly pointed to the Buddha-dharma at the start of the New Year: "Beating the wind and striking the rain, moving freely in all directions.

Leaning on his staff, he ascended the hall and said: "Today is the fifteenth day of the first month. Monastics and laypeople fill the gates and block the doors. As soon as the attendant announced that it was time to ascend the hall—"
The Wayman strikes the Dharma drum; the old monk comes out in a frantic rush. Who has time to cite the present or discuss the past?

Throughout his life he has disparaged all quarters; today, however, it is a scene of utter confusion. Great assembly, though there is indeed this confusion, you must know the timing and recognize what is appropriate before you can succeed.
It would be better to feign dumbness and pretend deafness, watching from a distance as they sing village songs and perform communal dances at the festival. Strike!
With the whisk, he descended from the seat.

He offered thanks to the two orders and ascended the hall. He opened the precious treasury and brought forth the family jewels, universally saving all sentient beings and causing them all to be fully satisfied.
The vajra circle and the chestnut thorn are both but common household utensils; they are simply like things that become precious when treated as base.
"Rising when encountering low points. Regarding the phrase "not harming the principle of things," how should one act? Let the steamed rice be fragrant as it may;
do not allow the ink to drip upon the paper robe.
Ascending the hall, he said: "On a clear spring day, the yellow orioles sing; various flowers bloom in profusion. Old trees stand tall and majestic.
A person stands upon a bridge over a verdant stream; as the water flows eastward, one listens for no sound. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
A monk asked the Master, "Riding the tiger's head and lashing the tiger's tail—what about the matter in between?
The Master said, "He has attained freedom. The monk asked, "As for what the ancients said, 'I too cannot bring it forth'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Entering the water, one sees the tall man."
The Master asked a monk, "If one can understand that which is within a single phrase and beyond two phrases, to what level of capacity does this belong? The monk prepared to respond;
the Master said, "To conceive of it is already an error; to open your mouth is to lose it. Begone!"
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bathing ceremony: The true Buddha has no form; what is there to bathe? Within the Lumbinī Garden, one perceives empty flowers through delusion.
If the command of Yunmen had been carried out, it would not have reached this day. Suddenly grasping his staff, he calls to the assembly, saying: "How shall we handle the matter of today?
One lost the sword in Kunming Lake, yet on the banks of the Qujiang River, one found a saw. He strikes the ground with the staff.

Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat: The ninety-day period of restraining the feet begins this very morning. I have ascended the hall specifically to provide guidance. When not a single thought arises, the three periods of time are severed;
the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are all fellow practitioners. Setting aside the matter of being a fellow practitioner for a moment, tell me: what is it?
Where do the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas dwell and establish their lives this very moment? (He strikes the whisk.
Holding the *yemingfu* talisman in his hand, how many know the break of dawn?
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Daowu asked Yunyan, "Having cast off this shell-like husk, where shall we meet?
Yunyan replied, "We shall meet in the place that is neither born nor extinguished. Daowu said, "Why not say we meet in the place that is *not* neither born nor extinguished?
The Master commented: "Neither born nor extinguished, and the place that is *not* neither born nor extinguished—both are entirely without form."
The *jianfen* (perceiving aspect). If someone were to ask Yunju, "Having cast off the shell and the leaky vessel, where do you meet?
he would simply say to him, "Where would we not meet? He would then suddenly pick up his staff, draw a line, and descend from his seat.
The Master asked a monk, "You have come such a long distance to attend upon this old monk.
In the future, on some other day, if someone were to ask me whether or not I have a way to benefit others, how would you answer? The monk prepared to speak, but the Master rebuked him, saying, "Go!
Do not say that you have ever seen this old monk."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In my place here, there is no Buddha-dharma to be preached, and no path of Chan to be studied.

You who have discoursed upon it elsewhere or mastered it through study must let it all go with your whole heart. With nothing to maintain within and nothing to rely upon without, you may well become a monk who is free and unencumbered.
At such a time as this, you must further know that there is a way to turn the body."
[He] finally attained it. [He] struck the whisk. "Red clouds pierce the azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Entering the hall, he said:
"The Dharma of the mind is formless, penetrating through the ten directions. In the ten directions there are no walls; on all four sides there is no obstruction."
"Pitiful is Master Fu; everywhere he loses his pavilions. Hanshan and Shide go even further, failing to find their own heads and noses.
Having said this, he descended from his seat.
After ascending the hall, following the conclusion of the summer retreat, he continued: "Go east, go west, go south, go north; you must head straight toward the highest of high mountains."
Standing at the summit. Walking upon the very bottom of the deep sea. If one cannot let go of things that belong to the inner chambers, one will inevitably fall into pits and ravines.
(He strikes the whisk. At the gate, he plants no more thorns, lest others come and catch hold of his robes.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Yunju had nothing he could do; he simply passed his time according to conditions. When hungry, he came for food and ate;

when weary, he stretched out his legs and slept. He could not practice Chan, nor did he know how to compose verses. Those who discourse on the profound and explain the subtle are all like donkeys pulling a millstone."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "When this old monk was clearing the wilderness, I dug up a blunt axe at the site of the Dharma Hall.
I have kept it for a long time, brothers; if there is anyone here who can make use of it, I shall entrust it to you with both hands.
But if you cannot carry its weight, I have already recovered it—why such a desperate hurry? It would be better to cast it onto a rubbish heap and let the sun scorch it day after day."
"The wind has blown it away. Suddenly picking up his staff, he strikes once and says: "Whipping up the iron ox to plow the great earth—who could plant crabapples at the bottom of a well?"
Opening the furnace, he ascended the hall. He cited the Venerable Zhaozhou, who pointed to the fire and showed it to the monks, saying, "I call this fire;
you must not call it fire. The Master said, "Old Zhaozhou, in his advanced age, still insists on stirring ashes and playing with fire.
At Yunju, it is otherwise: Together we surround the hearth and burn the fire; when host and guest reach accord, words are naturally forgotten."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within words there are words; this is called a 'dead phrase. Within words there are no words;
this is called a 'living phrase. How many people have died within the living phrase? How many people have lived within the dead phrase?
Furthermore, there is one person who can both die and live, sitting and cutting off all phrases, yet comes back to seek a staff from Yunju to eat. Because of this, he [spoke] to him."
"Stop! Do not be so hasty and reckless. Come tomorrow, and I shall bury you all in one pit. Why?
Because it is easy to distinguish flour from snow, but difficult to discern soot within ink."
"Master Yizang presides over the fire. That which comes and goes with you is the treasury; that which does not come and go with you is also the treasury.
You must clarify the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Be most careful not to fall under the power of others' words. With this, he struck a circle with his torch and said:
The moon does not depend on the wind to be cool; the sun does not depend on fire to be hot. [He] threw down a firebrand.
On the first day of the new year, he ascended the hall and said: "All insentient things possess Buddha-nature. Rising early in the morning, they celebrate the New Year.
If one bumps into a pillar in the Dharma Hall and pays it three prostrations, what is so wrong with that?

As for the mountain god of Anle Mountain, who for no reason is irritable and meddlesome, and the Venerable One who pats his own chest while prattling about right and wrong atop the foundation of the Buddha Hall—each shall receive twenty blows of the staff and be driven out beyond the pass of Zhaozhou.
Have you not heard it said: "The Three Thousand Articles of Law are administered by the Lord"?
This practice of giving should be selected by eminent monks.
Retiring from the monastery to ascend the hall, I have come to dwell among the clouds; five years have passed like a flickering candle.

My joy lies in forgetting external conditions, for my mind knows contentment within itself. Though empty fame cannot be escaped, a courier’s letter has reached this empty valley; I look upon it with a smile.
A broken-legged cauldron lies abandoned; upon whom can it rely for repair? I stroke this seven-foot rattan staff; its polished lacquer dazzles the eyes.
There is a time for using and a time for setting aside; why be bound by coming and going? Cherish this, you fellow travelers, and together sing the Song of Purity and Peace.
Suddenly grasping his staff, he calls to the assembly, saying: "Tell me, what tune is this Song of Purity and Peace? He gives a shout and descends from the seat.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume One;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Two.
Compiled by his disciples Zhijue and others.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month in the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, the Master entered the temple at Jingshan. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said:
"This Dharma-gate of mine is as vast as heaven and as broad as the earth. You all who enter and exit within it must know that there is a direction."
Only when you grasp the upper pivot will you succeed. (He gives a shout.
In the Buddha Hall, he burns incense and says: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are now, at this very moment where the incense smoke rises, emitting light and manifesting auspicious omens."
Turning the Great Dharma Wheel—foxes and white oxen break into loud laughter; the pillar and the lantern break into loud laughter. Taking his seat, he brandishes his staff and says:
"If it comes from the bright side, meet it at the bright side; if it comes from the dark side, meet it at the dark side.
If you can speak it, twenty blows with the staff; if you cannot speak it, twenty blows with the staff. Why? Under a heavy reward, there must be..."
There was a brave man who stood upright, leaning on his staff and holding up his paper.
This single phrase is inexhaustible for all the people in the great earth; today, this old monk has a share in its gratitude.
Regarding the position of the *zhǔzuò* (Presiding Seat): the former masters of old have ranked this office as the ultimate pinnacle.

When Zhāng the Presiding Seat perceived that it was merely ordinary, he ascended the seat; having offered incense and made his vow for the Emperor, he adjusted his robes and took his place. A monk asked:
"Receiving imperial grace from the Nine Heavens above, you occupy the Patriarchal Barrier atop the Five-Crested Peak; the Chan practitioners of the four seas all lean their ears toward you."

"I pray you will play a melody for the ten-thousand-year celebration. This student has come forward; I request the Master to lead the chant. The Master said, "Striking a golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru.
The student stepped forward and said, "In that case, a man of transcendent measure clarifies matters of transcendent measure; in times of great peace, one sings songs of great peace.
The Master said, "A difference of a hair’s breadth, and heaven and earth are as far apart. The student said, "The Master has traveled from afar."
"From the capital, I have recently arrived at Mount Jing. What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "Wait until Bowl Peak leaps up."
[The Master] said, "I shall tell you right now. Jin said, "I have just heard a statement in the preface: 'A thousand-year withered tree meets spring;
a single generation’s *tánhuá* manifests an auspicious omen. This may truly be called sincere speech. The Master said, "Why do you employ such a vast amount of consciousness and calculation?
Jin said, "On this day when the feast for dragons and elephants is spread, I have casually snatched the silken prize and returned. The Master said, "..."

"Not one of the guests of Longmen; take care not to suffer the 'dotted forehead'. He then said: "This mountain monk’s path is insufficient compared to the sages of old, and my traces are mingled with those of the monastic groves.

I simply let things take their course as time passes, cherishing the concealment of my own clumsiness. Who would have expected that the virtuous elders of the capital would mistakenly gather upon my hollow reputation?"
I was selected among the eminent monks and have humbly received the grace of the Holy Sovereign. Summoned to the Imperial Court, I personally received His Majesty’s wise praise;

a Dharma robe was specially bestowed upon me. I have brought glory to the ancestral tradition of Shaoshi, and as a mark of imperial favor, I have been appointed to preside over the seat of the First Patriarch of the National School.
As it is said within our teachings: "I originally had no mind to seek this; now this great treasure of the Dharma King has come to me of its own accord."
However, upon arriving at this time, my humble sentiments know only joy and gratitude.
As for what you say regarding the propagation of the Buddha-dharma and the repayment of the Imperial grace—how is the Buddha-dharma to be propagated, and how is the Imperial grace to be repaid?
Reaching this point, I wish for all of you to understand and realize it together. (He strikes the whisk. Ten thousand streams and a thousand brooks are all the Bohai Sea;

the seven golden mountains and five sacred peaks are all Mount Sumeru. He then spoke a verse: Personally receiving the imperial decree from within the Forbidden City, I sing of the profound mystery atop the Summit that Transcends the Clouds.
If one can entrust themselves to this single phrase of gratitude, They shall be among those chosen in the Field of Buddha-Selection.
Upon returning after passing the imperial examination, he ascended the hall on the winter solstice. Master Lu wrote "clouds" upon the dais; this is worldly dharma, not Buddha-dharma.
Master Ciming posted a notice before the hall; this is Buddha-dharma, not worldly dharma. Under the gate of Mount Jing, both Buddha-dharma and worldly dharma are brought forth.
Set this aside. Today the donor has prepared an offering; there is plenty of flatbread in the hall, so let everyone chew it as they please, whether horizontally or vertically.
Entering the hall: "When encountering a Buddha, kill the Buddha; when encountering an Ancestor, kill the Ancestor. Holding the Mohe sword crosswise, he scatters sand and dirt. I dare ask:
"O people! Since you have already laid your Mohe swords across your laps, why do you scatter sand and dirt?
Is it because this old fellow from Jingshan’s preaching of Chan lacks any scriptural authority? Turn the Southern Dipper back toward the North to look; the sun in the heavens is at its zenith."
During a session where a monk requested further instruction, the Master said, "In your own fundamental state, what is lacking that you come to request instruction?
As the monk was about to respond, the Master said, "You know only how to rush toward the goal, but fail to realize you have missed the way."
The Buddha ascends the hall after attaining the Way. He cites how the World-Honored One, before Mount Bodhi, beheld the morning star at night and attained the Unsurpassed Way, exclaiming:
"How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata;
it is only because of delusive thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it. The Master says: "I wish to ask Old Śākyamuni: what do you call this?"
This is the mark of wisdom and virtue. What do you call deluded thoughts and attachments? If you hesitate even for a moment, I strike you across the spine!
Is there anyone among this assembly who can avenge Śākyamuni Buddha? Holding up his staff, he said: "I do not dare hope that you will avenge Śākyamuni Buddha;
it would be well enough if you could simply find the nostrils of your own self. Rely on this!

How can we be blamed for this? [The Master] picks up his staff, draws a line, and says: "When the dust of the passions is exhausted, one sees the reality;
without passing through kalpas, one attains the Dharmakāya. Again, he cites a monk asking Dongshan: "When cold and heat arrive..."
"How do you avoid it? Dongshan said, "Why not go to a place where there is neither cold nor heat?
The monk asked, "What is the place where there is neither cold nor heat? Dongshan said, "When it is cold, it kills the *śrāmaṇera*;

when it is hot, it kills the *śrāmaṇera*. The verse says: "Facing him directly, one sees Dongshan; the orthodox and the deviant intermingle, yet they are not related. The place where there is neither cold nor heat is fit..."
Avoiding [distractions], that takes effort to reach a certain level.
A small *can* (sermon) for the summer retreat: Before the hall of the ancient Buddhas, there has never been any divergent path; at the gate of the Patriarchs, how could there be much talk?

However, the Buddha-dharma does not differ from the human mind; what one employs oneself is none other than the intent of the Patriarchs. This is truly due to the deluded views of acceptance and rejection, and of difference and sameness.
If one can directly accept and take responsibility for it, then one may immediately put it into practice at all times.

When the faculties and their objects are utterly detached, and the objective realm and wisdom are mutually integrated, then "this side" and "that side" are known only by oneself. Whether it be the True Dharma or the Semblance Dharma, they encompass all without being attached to them. If one were to divide...
To mistake mere conceptual understanding for the fundamental inquiry is another form of delusion; it is no different from trying to make a fine meal out of sand.
Have you not seen how the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, at the assembly on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, said to Ānanda:

"Though you have spent many kalpas in extensive learning, it is not equal to practicing the untainted study (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) for a single day. But how does one practice the untainted study? If you say there is something to it—

To claim there is cultivation and realization is precisely to deceive the common folk. To say there is neither speaking nor hearing is still to fall into the error of a coarse and superficial understanding of Buddha-nature.
All you practitioners of Chan: at this point, you must investigate with true substance; only by seeking decisive resolution from others can you succeed.
Tomorrow we shall enter the retreat, setting a fixed date for realization. Within these ninety days, do not treat this as a trivial matter. Time does not wait for anyone. Each of you—
"You should exert yourself. [He] strikes the whisk. Again, he cites Master Deshan’s informal discourse (*xiaocan*):

"Tonight’s informal discourse will not involve answering questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff. At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Deshan struck him immediately.
The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; why do you strike me? Deshan asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am from Xin..."
Master Luo said, "Before he has even stepped onto the gunwale of the boat, he deserves thirty blows.

The Master said, "Regarding this public case, whenever the venerable elders of all quarters encounter a small *can*, they cannot help but offer some critique. Yet, they are only able to support the strong; they cannot support the weak.
Tonight at Jingshan, I intend to settle this injustice. My teeth are like sword-trees and my mouth like a stone mortar; I shall restore it to him."
As for Old Man Deshan, if one were to judge his eye for discerning monks, he still lacked awakening.

Had that monk stepped forward at that moment and said directly, "I will not ask questions tonight; I simply wish to meet you, Master," and had Deshan then struck him, the monk would have seized the staff and sent him flying.
This would not only have cut off Deshan's momentum, but would also have proven that monk to be a truly swift and brilliant fellow.

The monk [responded]. The Master took up his staff and struck once. "A crane may have its nine-fold heights, yet its wings find it hard to soar; a horse may lack the thousand-li stride, yet it vainly pursues the wind.

This is the small *paramārtha* (private) discourse for the end of the summer retreat. The fruit of the Bodhi Way is fundamentally perfected of itself; it does not depend on cultivation, nor can it be obtained from others.
When the sentiments of both the holy and the common are exhausted, the true and eternal is revealed in its essence. It is manifest in every head and inherent in every object.
To understand and penetrate in this way is to see the source through to its root, to shatter the prison-barriers of birth and death, and to overturn the den of right and wrong.

Throughout the entire ten directions of the world, it is all one single monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*Samantabhadra*). Whether in a Buddha-land or a Mara’s palace, one plays freely according to conditions—even amidst brothels and taverns.
Free and easy, dwelling in the natural state, there is no distinction between defilement and purity; how could there be any difference between coming and going?
This is called the Ocean of Perfectly Complete Knowledge, and it is also called the Great Gate of Liberation. [The Master] suddenly picked up his staff, held it upright, and said:
"Śākyamuni Buddha, surrounded by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is right now upon the tip of this staff at Mount Jing. Spend the summer retreat here."
At ease. Each of you expounds the immeasurable and boundless subtle treasury of the Dharma. You people—do you not see without relying on two eyes?
Do you not hear without relying on two ears? If you have not yet seen or heard, you must by all means avoid attempting to calculate within empty space.
Leaning on the staff: when the wild goat hangs from its horns atop a thousand peaks, there is still another wild goat present.
At the beginning, [the Master] again cited Master Dongshan’s address to the assembly:

"In late autumn and early summer, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass. Many monks offered responses that did not accord with his intent.
One monk transmitted this to Shishuang, who said, "Why do you not say, 'As soon as you step out the door, it is already grass'? The monk then transmitted these words back to Dongshan.
Shan said, "In Liuyang, there is now an ancient Buddha appearing in the world. The Master offered this verse: "In the late autumn and early summer, I travel east and west;
A living path opens at the tip of my staff. For thousands of miles not a blade of grass grows, Yet as soon as I step out the door, it is a lush expanse of green."
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Da’an Zhuang, Volume Three;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Da’an Zhuang, Volume Four.
Compiled by his disciples Zhisheng and others.
The Ancient Case:

It is said that when a world-transcending sage with five supernatural powers questioned the World-Honored One, saying, "The World-Honored One possesses six supernatural powers, while I possess only five.
What is that one power? The Buddha called out to the sage. The sage with five powers responded. The Buddha said, "That one power—ask me about it."
The Master picks up the whisk and says: "The immortal asked well; the World-Honored One answered well. This may truly be called outshining the past and surpassing the future.
Yet, as for that one single penetration—none of you have even dreamed of it."
[The Master] raised the case of Venerable Ānanda asking Kāśyapa: "Venerable elder brother, besides the golden robe transmitted by the World-Honored One, what else did he transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. [The Master] comments:
"If you can understand it before the banner-pole has been thrown down, you bury the ancestral school. If you wait until the banner-pole has been thrown down..."
If you attain it later, you will have brought shame upon yourself. Now tell me: beyond the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One ultimately transmit?
A three-faced cat treads on the moon; a two-headed ox grasps smoke in its hands.

The Second Patriarch asked the Great Master Bodhidharma, saying, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace of mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you.
The Patriarch said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind."
The Master picks up [the case] and says: "To kill a person, one must have the sword that kills; to bring a person to life, one must have the sword that brings to life.
He cites the Sixth Patriarch: A monk asked, "Who can attain the essential meaning of Huangmei? The Patriarch said, "One who understands the Dharma of the Buddha can attain it.
The monk asked, "Can you, Master, attain it? The Patriarch said, "I cannot. The monk asked, "Why not, Master?"
“No. The Patriarch said, “I do not understand the Buddha-dharma. [The Master] remarked: “Whether one attains it or not, whether one understands it or not—let us not speak of those.
Why has the very life-essence of the Patriarch fallen into the hands of this monk? He struck his whisk and descended from the seat.
National Teacher Guoyi received a letter sent by Master Mazu. Inside the letter was a circle.
Upon opening the seal, Guoyi placed a dot within the circle and returned it sealed. Later, National Teacher Zhong heard of this and said, "Master Guoyi was still deluded by Master Ma.
[The commentator] remarks: "The arrow-points met directly; seizing and relinquishing were applied to the occasion. Do you understand?

He, Mazu, attained the beginning of the National Teacher’s [lineage]. Suddenly picking up his staff, he called to the assembly, saying, "As for the National Teacher’s words, 'Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma'—what, after all, was the meaning of this? He then struck the ground with his staff.
Master Mazu, while a monk was visiting him, drew a circle and said, "If you enter, I strike; if you do not enter, I strike. As soon as the monk entered, Mazu struck him.
The monk said, "Master, you may not strike me. Mazu leaned his staff against the wall and desisted. [The commentator] remarks:
Although the Great Master’s command was carried out, alas, he stirred up waves where there was no wind. Since this monk had already received the blow, [what more could be said?]
For now, there is a principle that is difficult to extend. He further asked: "How do you understand the principle of his 'resting'?
He cited Nanquan’s address to the assembly: "Wang Laozi is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy him?
At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and said, "I will buy him. Nanquan said, "Neither at a high price nor at a low price—how will you buy him?"

The monk had no reply. [Zhaozhou] picked up the case and said: "If I, this mountain monk, were that monk, when he said, 'I will not buy it at a high price nor at a low price,' I would have immediately replied to him:
'Venerable Sir, the horse's bridle reins are in the hands of so-and-so.
Even if Master Wang had some other special skill, he would have had to swallow his breath and remain silent."

Guizong once gave an instruction while leading the community in a communal work session to enter the garden to gather vegetables. He drew a circle around a single stalk of vegetable and drove a marker into the ground.
He said to the head seat and the assembly, "Do not touch it at all; each of you must offer a turning word.
At that time, the entire assembly presented their respective insights, yet none were in accord with his intent. Guizong chased them away with his staff, saying, "This..."
A group of men—none of them possessed a single bit of wisdom. Having devoured so much of my vegetables, they were unable to stand up for the gardener;
instead, they kicked over the stakes and dragged the vegetable stalks back with them. [The Master] picks this up and says:
"Even if a monk were to pull out one of those stalks of vegetables, would he be able to harmonize with Guizong? He takes up his staff, strikes the incense table, and says: "Guizong and..."
"He is still coming. [The Master] leans on his staff and cites Master Zhi:
"He sent someone to deliver a message to Dashi, saying: 'Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings?
Why do you merely gaze at the clouds and the Milky Way? Dashi replied: 'The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all been swallowed by me in a single mouth; where else could they possibly go?'"
"There are sentient beings who can be transformed. [The Master] raised his hand and said, "These two fellows—bury them both in one pit;
it would not be out of place. Nevertheless, one must not be careless. After a long silence, he said: "The clouds go toward the imperial capital; the waters flow from the Yangtze and Han rivers."
Yanguan raised up [a drum] and addressed the assembly, saying, "With space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet—what kind of person can beat it?
The assembly was silent. Nanquan said, "Old Teacher Wang does not beat this broken drum. [The Commentator] says: Nanquan spoke thus.
"Does the Salt Official still agree with him? I, this mountain monk, am not like that. Taking empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet—what kind of person could strike it?
Simply tell him: 'I do not decline to strike it; it is only that a true connoisseur is rarely encountered.'"
One day, as Panshan was going out his door, he saw a funeral procession being carried along. The songsters were shaking their bells and singing:
"The red wheel is certain to sink toward the west; we do not know where the soul has gone. Beneath the curtain, the filial sons wailed, "Alas! Alas! Suddenly, Panshan’s body and mind leaped with joy.
Upon returning, he related this to Mazu, who gave him his seal of approval. Mazu then remarked: "Now, one who acts as a teacher must..."
Possessing the eye that penetrates the barriers, one distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox to test the capacity of those who come.

Take for example Panshan, who took that which is "brightly manifest and spiritually alert" as the ultimate principle; when Mazu the Great Master subsequently certified him, was he not betraying the former sages and deceiving future generations?
In this place of mine, if there were such a person, they would surely have a different way of life—like a pair of mandarin ducks embroidered out.
From your perspective, he does not hand over the golden needle to others.
This refers to Yaoshan’s evening sermon, which said: "I have a phrase; I will tell it to you when a hornless ox gives birth to a calf."
At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "It is a bull giving birth to a calf. Yaoshan did not say anything. Yaoshan called to his attendant, "Bring a lamp!
The monk then withdrew and joined the assembly. [The Master] comments: "Great Yaoshan! You have the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
That monk knew only how to grasp at the moon, unaware of the depth of the water. To the assembly: "A bull giving birth to a calf—Yaoshan points this out to you."
The Master said, "Bring me a single phrase.
He then cited Chan Master Furong Yu: When Layman Pang asked Mazu, "Does your teacher transmit the place where he truly benefits people?
Furong replied, "I have not even seen him myself; how could I know his place of true realization?"
The layman said, "As for this very understanding, there is no place to seek it. Layman Rong said, "Layman, you must not speak in a one-sided manner.
The layman said, "If you speak in a one-sided manner, the Master has lost the essence. If you speak in two directions or three directions, would the Master still be able to open his mouth?
Layman Rong said, "It is as if he were opening his mouth, yet he cannot; this may be called reality. The layman clapped his hands and departed.

The Master picks up the staff and says: "Furong has, for no reason, stirred up much entanglement. From the perspective of my own view at Jingshan, I would simply give him a kick straight to the chest.
Even if Layman Pang had known the Master Mazu’s true ground, he still would not have been able to manage his hands and feet in time."

Regarding National Teacher Golden Ox: whenever he prepared food to offer to the assembly of monks, at every mealtime he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the Sangha Hall, perform a dance, and say, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat! Then he would clap his hands and laugh heartily. [The Master] comments:
The thief’s identity was already revealed. Master Pang raised this question for Mazu: "The person who is originally present is not obscure; I pray that you, Master, will look up with wide-open eyes.
Mazu looked straight down. Master Pang said, "This is a single stringless lute; only you, Master, can play it wondrously. Mazu looked straight up. Master Pang then made a gesture.
The Master returned to his quarters. The scholar followed him in and said, "To strive for cleverness is to produce clumsiness. The Master remarked, "I wish to ask Layman Pang:
what do you call the person of original nature? What is the stringless lute? He brandished his staff, saying, "It was not that I failed to let Master Mazu off;
it was simply that I did not wish to explain it all away. He struck the ground with the staff.
[The Master] raised the case of Yunyan asking Venerable Baizhang: "Every day you are busily occupied; for whom are you doing this?
Baizhang said, "There is one person who needs it. Yunyan said, "Why do you not let him do it himself? Baizhang said, "He has no means of living. [The Master] comments:
"A man of clear eyes cannot be deceived by even a single point. Do you understand? To wield [the Way], there is no need for a frost-sharpened blade; what need is there for longevity?"
Regarding the "Ninefold Elixir of Return," the story of Master Wujou is cited.
When the two senior monks Xuansha and Shaoshi came to visit him, Wujou asked, "Where did you two masters of Chan set out from?
Xuansha replied, "Jiangxi. Wujou raised his staff and struck him; Xuansha said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a capacity."

"Essential! Wuzhuo said. "Since you do not understand, look at the one who responds behind you. As Daochao prepared to step forward, Wuzhuo struck him and said, "Now you know that there is no difference in the soil within the same pit.
Go to the hall. [The Master] comments: On level ground lies a precipice; in the most solitary heights lies the plain.
Everywhere people only know that Wujiao possessed the means to transcend the school and surpass the standard, yet they do not know Wujiao...
Jiufu’s thorough grandmotherly heart—do you wish to recognize this grandmotherly heart? Striking the head of a stone man with a staff; *shao*, *shao*, discussing the actual matter.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "When two dragons struggle for the pearl, who is the one that gets it? Zhaozhou said, "I, this old monk, simply watch.
The Master [Zhaozhou] comments: "The strugglers do not get it; the one who gets it does not struggle. Zhaozhou simply watches, yet fundamentally he does not recognize the pearl."
To cite the case of Huangbo: When Baizhang asked him, "Where have you come from? Huangbo replied, "I have come from gathering mushrooms at the foot of the mountain.
Baizhang said, "Did you see the tiger? Huangbo then let out a tiger’s roar. Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to chop.
Huangbo then gave Baizhang a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned to the hall. Upon ascending the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying, "At the foot of Mount Daxiong, there is one..."
"Great tiger! You people must also watch carefully. Today, the old man Baizhang has personally met its fangs.
He then remarked: "Master and disciple attained one another; the needle and the magnet met. Their spiritual jabs were exchanged, and illumination and function proceeded in tandem.
It was like two dragons contending for a pearl, clawing through clouds and mist without stirring a ripple; like two tigers fighting over food, seizing the prey alive."
One does not harm the lives of sentient beings. As it is said: "Baizhang lacked the mechanism for trapping tigers; Huangbo possessed the capacity to transcend his teacher.
To discuss the matter in such a manner is like piercing the brain and plunging it into a vat of glue. [With this] whisk, he draws a single stroke:
he splits apart Mount Hua, with its peaks reaching to the heavens in splendor, and releases the Yellow River, pure to its very depths.

Dongshan addressed the assembly, saying: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, whether you go east or west, you must go to a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass before you will succeed.
But as for that place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there?
A monk brought this up to Shishuang, who said: "As soon as you step out the door, it is all grass. The Master [Zhaozhou] took up his staff and said: "Everyone goes right into the grass."
Rolling it on. What end can there ever be? [Heh]! Holding up his staff, he said: "I cite Zhaozhou.
Once a monk asked him, 'I have newly entered this monastery; I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, 'Have you finished eating your congee?
The monk replied, 'I have finished. Zhaozhou said, 'Go wash your bowl. Because of this, the monk attained awakening."
Yunmen said, "Now tell me: was there an instruction or not? If you say there was, what did Zhaozhou say to him?
If you say there was not, why did that monk attain awakening? [The Master] comments: Zhaozhou used a wedge to drive out a wedge;
Yunmen watched the tower and struck the tower. As for that monk attaining awakening—was there any room for examination or not? After a long silence: "The wind does not whistle through the branches."
"Rain does not break the clods.
This refers to the occasion when a monk traveling to Mount Wutai asked an old woman, "Where does the road to Mount Wutai lead?
The woman said, "Go straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked three or five paces, the woman said, "What a fine monk! And yet, you act like this... [The text ends here].
[The monk] went away. Later, a monk reported this to Master Zhou. Master Zhou said, "Wait, I shall examine this old woman for you.
The next day he went there and asked the same question; the old woman answered in the same way. Upon returning, Master Zhou said to the assembly, "The old woman of Mount Tai."
I have thoroughly investigated and seen through this. He held up his staff and said: "Everyone in the assembly says that Zhaozhou saw through the old woman;
little do they realize that it was actually the old woman who saw through Zhaozhou."
Muzhou raised this up and addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, if you have not yet attained an entry point, you must attain one.
If you do attain an entry point, do not fail me, the old monk. [The Master] commented: "Great Muzhou is covered head to toe in mud and water.
I do not act in this way. He then called out to the assembly in a stern voice, "Step back! Step back! As the assembly hesitated, [the Master struck them].
[The Master] picks up his staff and drives them all out at once.
He cites the case of Yangshan: while Yangshan was sitting, Da Chanfo arrived and stood on one foot, saying, "The twenty-eight patriarchs of India were like this;
the six patriarchs of the Land of Tang were like this; the Master was like this; and I am also like this. Yangshan [said], "..."
He descended from his meditation seat and struck four blows with his staff, then said: "Aspidium is without the real; mercury is without the false.
He then cited Deshan’s address to the assembly: "To ask is to have a fault; not to ask is to be at variance. At that moment, a monk came forward and paid his respects.
Deshan struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; why do you strike me?
Deshan replied, "If I wait for you to open your mouth, what use would it be? [The Commentator] says: Deshan held the authority in his hand, executing life or death as the occasion required.
This monk had long been a veteran of the battlefields, fighting with reckless disregard for his own body. Nevertheless, even so, it cannot be said that both were fully resolved. Is there anyone else?
How could one who has fundamentally attained it be like this? True gold naturally has the price of true gold; it is never sold to others mixed with sand.
[The Master] cites Linji’s ascent of the hall: A monk stepped forward; Linji immediately shouted. The monk also shouted; he then bowed. Linji struck him. [The Master] comments:
It is like the water jellyfish, which has no eyes and must rely on the bright eyes of a shrimp to seek food. A patch-robed monk should certainly be able to discern this.
[The Master] took it up. He cited the case where a monk asked Touzi: "Vaguely it resembles a half-moon; faintly it is like three stars. Heaven and earth cannot contain it;
in what place does the Master clarify it? Touzi said, "What are you saying? The monk said, "I imagine the Master possesses only the stillness of a deep pool..."
"Ripples, yet no waves that flood the heavens. The Master said, "Idle talk. [The Commentator] says: Suppose someone were to ask this; I, too, would say, "What do you mean?
When he replied, "There are only ripples on still water, yet no waves that flood the heavens," I would strike him a painful blow right at his heels.
[The Commentator] picks up his staff and says, "Is there anyone? Is there anyone? He leans on the staff.
It is said: "Even if one were to cultivate it thoroughly, it would not be timber for a ridgepole.
Cao Shan was asked by a monk: "A student brings his raw jade to the Master; I pray the Master will polish it. Cao Shan said: "I do not polish it. The monk asked:
"Why do you not polish it? Cao Shan said: "You must know that Cao Shan is a master craftsman. [The Commentator] says: Now tell me—what do you say?
This refers to the words of Cao Shan that Zeng Hui did not understand. As for Cao Shan’s words, I, this mountain monk, say: even if you were to understand them, it would still be groundless.
He cites Xinghua ascending the hall and saying: "Today, there is no need for 'how' or 'what. I ask you simply to enter directly with a single blade."
Xinghua provided you with evidence. At that time, the Elder Minde came forward to pay his respects; as he rose, he gave a shout.
Xinghua also shouted. Minde shouted again; Xinghua shouted again. Minde bowed and returned to the assembly.

Xinghua said, "If it had been anyone else just now, thirty blows of the staff would not have been too much—nor would even a single blow have been spared—for Minde understood the shout as not being a mere shout."
[The Master] uses [the verse]. He holds it up and says: "These two venerable masters—one buys a hat to fit the head, the other scratches an itch through a boot.
Although these were expedient measures for a single occasion, how can they avoid being mutually obstructive? Why? To see what is right and not act upon it—what bravery is there in that?"
Juyongquan (Yǒngquán) was visiting Xuefeng (Xuěfēng). As he was seeing him off at the gate, Xuefeng entered his sedan chair.

Yǒngquán said, "This one is carried by four people; which one is carried by how many? Xuefeng then leaped up from the chair and said, "What are you saying? Yǒngquán asked again. Xuefeng said, "He does not understand.
Yǒngquán said, "If he knows, he knows; it is simply that he cannot speak of it. [The Master] comments: There is a master; there is a host.
The guest: Total gathering and total letting go—you must directly recognize Yongquan and Xuefeng.
If this is not yet the case, you must by all means avoid driving stakes into empty space.
Yantou’s encounter with Deshan is cited: as soon as he stepped across the threshold, he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it sacred? Deshan gave a shout; Yantou bowed.
Upon hearing this recounted, Dongshan said, "If it were not for Old Man Huo, it would have been very difficult to handle.
Yantou said, "Old Man Dongshan does not know good from bad; he has wrongly applied a name and phrase. At that time, I was holding up with one hand while pressing down with the other."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Deshan was not without the karmic conditions for raising a son; Dongshan was merely celebrating the feast.
What is it that Yantou does with one hand lifting and one hand pressing down? This is no archer’s hand; it is like those who speak in vain of General Li."
Jue Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying: "To awaken to the Way upon hearing sound; to clarify the mind upon seeing form.
What is it to awaken to the Way upon hearing sound and clarify the mind upon seeing form? He then said: "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara buys sesame cakes with money;
when he lets go of his hand, they turn out to be steamed buns. [The Master] commented: "I am not like Yunmen, who mistakes the servant for the master and points to a deer while calling it a horse."
Suddenly picking up his staff, he said, "Look! Look! This staff pierces through the skulls of you all. He struck the ground with the staff.
He cited the case of Xuan Sha, when Attendant Guang said, "If you, Master Uncle, understand Chan, I shall build an iron boat and sail out to sea.
After Xuan Sha took up residence there, he sent someone to deliver a letter asking Guang, "Have you built the iron boat yet? [The Master] commented: "This..."
Regarding this koan, there have been no small number of critics from all quarters; yet they are only able to support the strong and cannot support the weak.

Today, I, this mountain monk, have long investigated it and find it does not deviate from its original form. I dare say that Xuansha was led astray by Attendant Guang, such that he could not even properly analyze the matter.
After all, how is it? When the government has no fixed statutes, one follows the private conventions of the people.
Juyan was once asked by a monk, "On this ball of raw flesh, it stands like a thousand-fathom cliff—is this not the Master’s own words?
Juyan replied, "Yes. The monk then overturned the meditation seat. Juyan said, "Look at this blind fellow making such a mess!
As the monk hesitated, Juyan struck him out. The Master commented: "Under a heavy reward, there will surely be brave men."
Changqing raised [the case] and said, "In general, it seems that today the Old Barbarian still has expectations. [The Master] commented: "Gold is tested by stone.

Baofu said, "In general, it seems that today the Old Barbarian has lost all hope. [The Master] commented: "Jade is tested by fire. He struck his whisk and said: "One year of spring has already passed;
the terraces and pavilions are filled with lush green shade."
Citing Fengxue: A monk once asked, "When speech and silence involve transcendence and subtlety, how can one pass through them without transgression?
Fengxue replied, "I always remember that in the third month of Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant. The Master [Zhaozhou] comments:
This monk asked in such a manner, and Fengxue answered in such a manner; it is similar, yet it is not yet correct. Nevertheless, if you wish to see this Fengxue, look!
"Sixty kalpas in three lifetimes.
He raised his head and held up a bamboo staff to the assembly, saying, "To call it a bamboo staff is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a bamboo staff is to turn one's back. What do you all call it? Ye Xian Sheng stepped forward, seized it, broke it in two, and threw it away.
He went toward the foot of the steps and asked, "What is it? Shanshan said, "Blind! Xian then prostrated. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented:
"To possess such total elegance, one must be like Shoushan when facing an opponent. It was only to Ye Xian that he could proceed consistently in this manner;
otherwise, the Buddha-dharma of Linji would have been swept away to its very foundations."
Juefeng Yang addressed the assembly, saying, "If you recognize this staff, the business of traveling on pilgrimage is finished. [The Master] added:
"Fen-yang’s single staff has replaced the eyes of all the patch-robed monks in the world."
Master Songyuan, when nearing his death, addressed the assembly, saying: "There are those who have long gathered on the path of the orthodox way, yet they cannot employ the 'black bean' method;
thus it is difficult to shoulder the true lineage. The Buddha-dharma of Linji has reached this point of sinking into oblivion.
How painful, how painful! [The commentator] adds: Master Songyuan, the great ancestor, was treating the noble as common. Had he been able to employ the 'black bean' method, there would have been...
"How extraordinary! You must take the rope for binding and pass it through the nostrils of all the Buddhas and patriarchs from above;
only then will you have a share of true freedom. At that time, a monk said, "Is the rope for binding not in the Master's hand? The Master said, "You blind fellow!
He took up his staff and struck him.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Four;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Five.
Compiled by his disciples De-xiu and others.
In a verse on an ancient precedent, it is related that one day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The verse says:
Mañjuśrī struck the gavel; the World-Honored One descended from his seat. The pillar and the lantern have clearly explained it all—do you, my fellow monks, understand this thoroughly?
When the water rises, the boat floats higher; when the mud is deep, the Buddha is great.
The World-Honored One was once questioned by a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). The questioner asked neither whether there is speech nor whether there is no speech.

The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, sitting upright in his seat. The non-Buddhist praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One’s great compassion has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter [the Way].
Having paid homage, he departed. Later, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What did that non-Buddhist realize that he could depart with such praise? The Buddha said:
It is said: "Like a fine horse of the world that gallops upon seeing the shadow of the whip. The verse says:
"Regardless of whether there is silence or speech, The celestial long sword’s precious light is cold.
Why wait for the shadow of the flickering whip? Ānanda was pointlessly deceived by the heat."
It is said that when the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he held up a flower to show the multitude.

At that time, the assembly was all at a loss, except for the Venerable Kāśyapa, who broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa;
I entrust them to Mahākāśyapa."
At the place where he showed the flower to the assembly, when his face broke into a smile, the million followers on Vulture Peak were all struck with wonder and doubt.
To cite Master Bodhidharma: once, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked him, "What is the primary meaning of the holy truths?"
The Master said, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Master replied, "I do not know.
The Emperor did not attain realization, so the Master broke off a reed and crossed the river.
The Hu monk has missing teeth and a long tongue; how could his speech possibly accord with that of the Emperor?
Having broken off a stalk of reed, he crosses the river—thus it is known there is no place for shame.
To cite the Sixth Patriarch Master: once, when a wind blew a flagpole, two monks debated it. One said, "The wind moves. The other said, "The banner moves.
After much back-and-forth, neither had yet realized the principle. The Master said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves."
The benevolent one’s mind was stirred; the two monks were struck with awe.
"It is neither the wind nor the banner. With a turn of the body, he breaks through ten thousand layers of barriers. He smiles as he gazes upon the full moon in the sky;
its reflection falls into the clear pool, chilling to the very bottom.
To cite National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang: One day he called his attendant three times. The attendant responded with "Yes" three times.
The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you; it turns out it was you who failed me."
If you can understand the three calls and three responses, why speak of "carrying me" or "carrying you"? One who bites rarely encounters a lion;
those who chase clods of earth are mostly seen to be *hanlu* hounds.
Regarding Mazu, Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan, while they were enjoying the moon, Mazu said: "Right at this very moment..."
"How is it now? the Hall Master asked. Baizhang said, "It is precisely the time for cultivation. Nanquan said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings.
Nanquan then shook his sleeves and departed. The Patriarch said, "The Sutras enter the Canon; Chan returns to the Sea. Only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world."
When playing with the moon before Mazu’s hall, the three brothers each displayed their wits. Their shared ugliness was impossible to conceal;
how could bystanders avoid commenting on their faults?
Regarding Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu: When Mazu saw him approaching, he held up his whisk. Baizhang said, "Is it the function itself, or is it separate from the function?
Mazu hung the whisk back in its original place and remained silent for a long while, then asked, "After this, when you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth], with what will you teach people?
Baizhang also held up his whisk. Mazu said, "Is it the function itself, or is it separate from the function?"
Baizhang also hung his whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, which left Baizhang deaf for three days straight.
Later, when Huangbo came to study with him, the Patriarch raised this incident; Huangbo then stuck out his tongue.
Picking up and letting go, there is no need for much contention; father and son walk together through the grass.
A single shout that deafens the ears is easy to understand, but the tongue that has been spat out is most difficult to clarify.
It is said that Mazu was unwell. The head of the monastery asked him, "How has your health been lately, Master?
Mazu replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face;
appearing in response to every direction, the sun-faced and moon-faced. For a monk with eyes, what is there that is difficult to see? This morning, after the rain has passed..."
The wind stirs upon the Yangtze River; reeds line both banks. [The Master] cites Nanquan:
Once, when the two head monks of the two halls were disputing over a cat, Nanquan held it up and said, "If you can speak, you shall save it;
if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. The assembly was speechless, and Nanquan subsequently killed it. That evening, Zhaozhou—
Upon returning from outside, Nanquan presented this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and walked out.
Nanquan said, "If you had been here, you would have saved the cat."
When Yang lifts up the cat, if he can explain it clearly, he may save him. With a single stroke, he cuts him in two;
even to emerge wearing straw sandals would be in vain.
Master Lu Xun asked Nanquan, "Dharma Master Zhao is truly extraordinary;

he can explain that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are one body. Nanquan pointed to the peony in the courtyard and said, "Master, when people of this age see this single flower, it is like a dream."
Are heaven and earth of the same root? Pointing it out before the courtyard, there is the peony flower. Holding gold, he sells it along with the sand;
who would say Nanquan was not a master?
One day, Salt Official (Yanguan) called to his attendant and said, "Bring me my rhinoceros fan.
The attendant replied, "The fan is broken. The Official said, "Since the fan is broken, bring me back the rhinoceros.
The attendant was speechless.
The rhinoceros horn fan is broken; he seeks the rhinoceros again. This old fellow of Yanguan is truly shameless.
[It is said that] whenever Lu Zu saw a monk approach, he would simply face the wall.
When Luzu saw a monk, he did nothing but face the wall; what use was there for the Master’s mouth to chatter away?
It is no wonder that in days of yore, the Elder of Vaiśālī engaged in dialogue with Mañjuśrī alone.
To cite the story of Deshan’s first meeting with Longtan: Deshan immediately asked, "I have long heard of Dragon Pond;
yet now that I have arrived, neither the pond nor the dragon is to be seen. Longtan replied, "You have personally arrived at Dragon Pond."
For a thousand ages, the waters of Longtan have been vast and boundless. When Deshan arrived in person, what more was there to doubt?
With eyes upon the crown of his head as bright as the sun, he remained entirely unaware of the deep mud beneath his feet.
Once, when Danxia arrived at a desolate monastery during the night, he took a wooden Buddha and burned it over a fire.
The monastery master rebuked him, saying, "How can you burn my wooden Buddha? Danxia struck the fire with his staff and said, "I am burning for its relics."
The abbot said, "How could a wooden Buddha have *śarīra*? Xiang replied, "If it has no *śarīra*, bring two more and burn them.
Subsequently, the abbot's eyebrows and beard fell out.
Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; the temple steward lost his eyebrows and beard. Having removed the speck from the eye, he adds another thorn behind the head.
It is said that one day Zhaozhou visited Zhunyu and, holding his staff, paced back and forth across the Dharma Hall.
Nanyue said, "What are you doing? Xiangzhou said, "I am probing the water. Nanyue said, "In my place here, there is not even a single drop.
Xiangzhou leaned his staff against the wall and departed.
Zhaozhou probes the waters at Zhuyou; how could he have known there was not even a single drop? At that time, he leaned his staff against the wall;
what was clear and direct became, instead, a detour.
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dongshan said, "Wait until the waters of the Dong River flow backward, and then I will tell you.

A master’s opening of his mouth leaves no room for sentiment; he desires only that the person act with genuine reality. Until the waters of the Dong River flow backward, [the answer] can never be given.
Wait. Who will clarify the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
[The Master] raised the case of Yangshan asking Zhongyi: "How can one attain the vision of one's nature? Zhongyi said: "Suppose there is a room with six windows.
Inside is a monkey, and outside is a monkey. From the east, someone calls out, 'Singing-sing! The monkey [inside]...
The monkey immediately responded. Thus, when called simultaneously at all six windows, the monkey responded to each.

Daowu bowed in thanks and said, "I have now understood everything through the Honored One’s parable. However, there is one further matter: what happens when the inner monkey is dozing while the outer monkey wishes to see it?
Daowu took Yangshan’s hand, led him to the meditation seat, and performed a dance, saying, "A langur! (xiōng).
The monkey has met you;
his questions were intimate and his answers were clear. His modulation was measured, and the rhythm of call and response proceeded in tandem.
Whether the macaque is drowsy or not, it is precisely at these six windows that one should summon the *xingxing*.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
This decrepit Zhaozhou is utterly victorious over all adversaries; whether he conceals his point or bares his blade is entirely up to him. He points directly at the cypress in the courtyard.
Bai: How does this compare to meeting a monk and calling out, "Have some tea"?
[The Master] cites a story from the past: there was an old woman who supported a hut-dweller for over twenty years, sending a young girl of eighteen to deliver food and attend to him.
One day, she ordered the girl to embrace him firmly and asked, "At this very moment..."
"How is it? the Master said. "A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff; for three winters there has been no warmth. The woman returned and reported this to her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law said, "In twenty years of providing offerings, I have only managed to support a worldly fellow.
She then drove him out and set fire to the hut, burning it to the ground.
The story of the Old Woman Burning the Hermitage. Zen practitioners, look closely! No warmth in the three months of winter; snow and frost in the sixth month.
Jingding Shouzhang asked Linji, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Linji descended from his rope bed, seized him, and gave him a slap, then pushed him away.
Jingding stood there motionless. A monk standing nearby said, "Shouzhang, why do you not bow?"
Prostrations. A ritual performed at a fixed time; suddenly, there was great awakening.
The meeting between teacher and disciple is certainly no trivial matter. I tell you all, strive to understand clearly:
beside the red peony, the butterflies dance; within the green wutong tree, the orioles sing.
Xuefeng raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying: "The entire earth is gathered up and made as small as a grain of millet;
it is tossed before you. You lacquer buckets do not understand! Let us strike the drum and invite everyone to look!"
The great earth is gathered up like a grain of millet; looking upon it casually, one’s very hair stands on end with cold. Xuefeng bestows compassion for the sake of sentient beings;
let the drum be beaten so that all may come to see.
A monk raised this story: A monk asked Dao Wu, "What is the Master’s profound depth?
Dao Wu descended from his meditation seat, performed a woman's bow, and said, "Thank you for coming from afar; I have nothing to offer as a host."
Directly pointing to the deepest depths, he returns [the teaching] to the man who transcends [the mundane]. Descending from his seat, he performs a woman’s bow, waiting with even greater sincerity.
He cites Lingyun’s realization upon seeing peach blossoms, for which there is a verse: "For thirty years I have sought a swordsman;
Several times the leaves fell and branches sprouted anew. Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, To this very day, I have not looked back."
Doubtful. Later, when Xuansha heard of this, he said: "How perfectly true! How truly perfect! I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the end.
Once the peach blossoms were seen, there was no further doubt; yet Lingyun’s eyes—large or small—were but a film of rheum. This brings laughter to the guests upon the fishing boat;
for no reason at all, he plucks leaves and seeks branches again.
When Linji was about to pass away, he entrusted his successor, Sansheng, saying, "After I have departed this world, you must not let my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be extinguished.
Sansheng replied, "How would I dare let it be extinguished? Linji said, "If someone were to ask you, 'What would you say?
