how would you respond? Sansheng then gave a shout. Linji said, "Who knew that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be entrusted to such a blind donkey?"
It is extinguished at the periphery.

With a shout, life and death are fully manifested; before the pivot of action, one must distinguish the orthodox from the biased. Who would have known that the Eye of the True Dharma was extinguished within the jaws of a blind donkey?
Yunmen raised his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "This staff transforms into a dragon and swallows up heaven and earth."
It is understood. Where did these mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?
Yunmen’s staff has transformed into a dragon; it swallows up heaven and earth with utter ease.
Had I seen this, I would have surely snapped it in two, lest it continue to peer through a keyhole at a mere fragment of the whole.
To cite Touzi: When a monk asked, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? the Master descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
Again the monk asked, "How far apart are the ordinary person and the sage? The Master likewise descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
Failing to truly strike the tiger, one’s efforts are in vain as the arrow feathers sink. To hold it up from above, one must return to Touzi.
Pity those who chase after people throughout the world; five times five remains twenty-five.
Citing a monk’s question to Dongshan: “What is the Buddha? Dongshan replied, “Three catties of hemp.
From the beginning, both life and death have been entirely free; the weapons of war on all three sides are gathered up at once.
Who knows that without employing any stratagems, one sits firmly pacifying the four hundred prefectures of the Central Plains?
Citing Master Zhaozhou, he said: "All people are driven by the twelve periods of the day; I, the old monk, drive the twelve periods of the day.
This ancient, sharp-tongued Zhaozhou drives the twelve periods of the day—on his bed, broken reeds; in his hand, coarse and pungent pears.
A monk asked Fengxue, “What is the Buddha? Fengxue said, “Under the Zhangling Mountain, bamboo-stalk whips.
Under the Zhangling Mountain, bamboo-stalk whips. How can one bring forth this single phrase in its entirety? It is a golden ball cast from raw iron;
a man from Fusang plows the fields of Shanxi.
Regarding Master Yinyuan of the Tang Dynasty: while he was still a youth, he was once carrying a hammer to strike clods of earth.
Upon seeing a particularly large clod, he playfully struck it with great force; as it shattered, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
Later, an elder heard of this and said, "The entire mountain, rivers, and great earth have been reduced to a hundred fragments by a single blow from Master Yinyuan."
A single blow shatters them into a hundred fragments; the myriad phenomena all rejoice in their liberation. As for the Great Master Yindu, what kind of clod of earth is he?
[The Master] raised the case: A monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu said, "This very mind is the Buddha.
Again, a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? Mazu said, "Neither mind nor Buddha."
To say "mind is Buddha" constitutes a false view; to say "neither Buddha nor mind" involves much more deluded turning. Cast aside these two sets of locks and pivots;
in great peace, what need is there to brandish weapons?
Citing the Three Barriers of Chan Master Huanglong Nan, the verse says:

"What is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? Lift it up and you should immediately know there is something beyond. Casually squeezing through empty space, It is precisely the time to hide one's body in the Big Dipper."
"What are my feet like? They are like donkey's feet!"—one can speak thus without hindrance. You must believe that Zhaozhou’s Stone Bridge is not like an ordinary footbridge.
Every person has their own karmic affinity;
if you understand it, it is right before your eyes. Not recognizing Hanshan and Shide, you call them... [by other names].
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra raised the case of National Teacher Niaoke, who, because of the attendant Huìtōng, took his leave to travel to various regions to study the Buddha-dharma.
The Master said, "As for the Buddha-dharma, we have a little here as well. Huìtōng asked, "What is this 'here'?"
Regarding this matter of the Buddha-dharma, the Master took a tuft of cloth from his robe, blew upon it, and showed it to him; thus he attained great enlightenment.
Its daily manifestation is clear and vivid; yet as soon as one attempts to direct the mind toward it, it becomes obscured.
There was nothing much in that blowing of the cloth-tuft—it simply required that you look with your own eyes.
Master Wuzu Yan was once asked by a monk in his quarters: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants;
tell me, who is he?"
It cannot be described, nor can it be painted; the face given by one's mother is perfectly clear. Let it fill the void as it may;
do not call it by its childhood nickname before others anymore.
Chan Master Juyoue of Tushita established three barriers and questioned his students, saying: "You who pull weeds to investigate the profound seek nothing but the realization of your nature.
Where, then, is your original nature right now? Only by recognizing your own nature can you escape birth and death."
When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, how does one achieve liberation? If one can liberate oneself from birth and death, then one will know the place of departure.
When the four elements separate, where does one go?
In the morning one eats congee; at the midday meal one eats rice. Two fives make ten;
buying high and selling low, subtracting a little and adding much. If you wish to know Li Si, ask Zhang San.
Carrying dry wood with him, he performs his play wherever the stage meets him. The bright sun adorns the heavens; the clear breeze circles the earth.

When Deshan arrived at Weishan, he took his *fuzi* (a staff with a ring) into the Dharma Hall, walked from west to east and from east to west, looked around and said, "Nothing, nothing," and then departed. Upon reaching the gate, Deshan spoke again: "It is so."
"One must not be careless. Thus, he prepared his formal demeanor and entered again for an audience.
While Guishan was seated, Deshan held up his sitting mat and said, "Preceptor! Guishan reached for his whisk, whereupon Deshan let out a shout, shook out his sleeves, and departed.
With his back turned to the Dharma Hall, he put on his straw sandals and left. That evening, Guishan asked the Head Seat, "Just now..."
"A newcomer has arrived. "Where is he? The Head Seat replied, "At that time, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went out wearing straw sandals.
Guishan said, "This fellow will later go to the summit of a solitary peak, build a grass hut, and there he will revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs."
The precious mirror upon the stand tests the true master; when Deshan glanced at it, his eyes saw flowers. Turning his body, he sat firmly atop the solitary peak;
with one flavor, he scattered earth and sand whenever he met people.
A monk asked Zen Master Zhaozhou, "Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses?
Zhaozhou replied, "It is like striking a ball on a swift current. The monk then asked Touzi, "What is the meaning of 'striking a ball on a swift current'?
Touzi said, "Thought after thought, it flows without ceasing."
On the rapids of a swift torrent, he plays with a ball; who would say that every thought-moment flows without ceasing?
Amidst the vast expanse of the six directions where people are like the sea, one who is free and elegant in every way is Zhaozhou.
Citing Zhaozhou’s question to Touzi: “When a person who has undergone the great death returns to life, what is it like? Touzi said:
“Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive at dawn.”
To find life within death is likewise not permanent; one must by all means avoid raising such matters in error before others. Last night, facing south, I gazed at the Northern Dipper;
without moving my heels, I arrived home.
A monk asked Dàlóng, "The physical body perishes; what is the indestructible Dharma-body?
Lóng said, "Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; mountain stream water is as deep blue as indigo."

Mountain flowers resemble brocade; mountain waters are like indigo dye. One must strictly avoid following words and falling into duality or plurality. The firm Dharma-body has been pointed out and noted;
though the Great Dragon possesses a mouth, it should remain sealed in silence.
When Juy Tianping was traveling as a wandering monk, he visited Xiyuan. He used to say, "Let alone understanding the Buddha-dharma;
there is not even a single person to be found who can raise a koan. One day, Xiyuan saw him from afar and called out, "Congyi!
Tianping raised his head. Xiyuan said, "Wrong. Tianping walked two or three steps forward. Xiyuan said again, "Wrong. Tianping approached him.
West Hall said, "Those two previous mistakes were both West Hall’s mistake and the Senior Monk’s mistake. Pingshan said, "They were mistakes from the very beginning.
West Hall said, "Mistake! Pingshan then withdrew. West Hall said, "Stay here for the summer retreat;
let us deliberate together on these two mistakes. At that time, Pingshan departed immediately. Later, when he was presiding over a monastery, he said to the assembly, "In the beginning..."
While traveling on foot, I was driven by the wind to the abode of the Elder Siming.
There, I made two consecutive mistakes, and he further invited me to stay for the summer retreat, saying he wished to deliberate with me. I did not say it was a mistake at that time;
rather, I knew it was a mistake long ago when I first set out for the South.
A traveling monk from Tianping arrived at Xiyuan. Alas, how could one avoid making two mistakes? We waited together to deliberate on staying for the summer retreat;
yet to this day, those who misunderstand are beyond counting.
Baoshou was inaugurating the hall. Sanxing pushed forward a monk, and Baoshou struck him immediately.
Sanxing said, "To act as a teacher in such a manner will not only blind this monk's eyes, but will also blind the people of the entire city of Zhenzhou."
Baoshou cast down his staff and descended from the seat.
In the turning of the wheel of his hand, he fully employed both killing and giving life; at the tip of his staff, illumination and function must be clearly distinguished.
Truly, he blinded the eyes of the people of an entire city and brought shame upon the ancestral wind of the two brothers.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the pure dharmakāya? Yunmen said, "A flower garden railing.
The monk asked, "How is it when one goes directly like this? Yunmen said, "A golden-maned lion."
From within the midst of nothingness, the ancient Yunmen proclaims; with every stroke, his timing is fresh and his tune renewed.
Though the flower garden is easy to see, how can it compare to hiding one’s body within the Northern Dipper?
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Five.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Six.
Compiled by the junior disciples Tandong and others.
A verse presented to Chief Seat Jing:
Muzhou succeeded Huangbo; Lingshu awaited Yunmen. Such a person is an eye of heaven and earth; his radiance illuminates the universe.
The mechanism seizes the mechanism; the wedge drives out the wedge. Who can distinguish between the contrary and the compliant, the vertical and the horizontal?

When master and disciple meet, they are like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a hen and her chick. Guest and host forget one another as the rhythm of striking and singing falls into harmony. Seizing the profound pivot, the true command is enacted. Who in later generations shall succeed this peerless purity?
You, Venerable One, are naturally of the ranks of the eminent and talented; in your prime, your ambition and spirit pierce the Dipper and Ox constellations.
Beneath Mount Jiyun, he shared half his seat; his grand vision was vast, emulating the masters of old.

Leading disciples on pilgrimage across rivers and seas, he investigated all quarters with a sincerity that left nothing unmet. Shaking out his traveling bag, he possessed not a single thing; yet the seven-foot black staff remained in his hand.
Having come to visit me amidst the deep clouds, our conversation reached the wordless state where the mind is at ease. He drew forth [the sword] from the Qin era...
Crushing and piercing with a chariot wheel; casually leaning over and toppling Mount Sumeru.
To send forth a phrase prior to the birth of the Buddha for the Wheel-Treasury Abbot, I spare not my eyebrows to raise it for you: as soon as the mouth opens, it clearly falls into duality.

3. Stop up your faculty of hearing and listen! How degenerate the Way of the Dharma has become today! They discourse on the profound and speak of the wondrous, boasting of their transmission and maintenance.
How many are there among the Han-lu hounds that merely chase after clods? Rarely do we see a lion cub that bites.

Have you not seen how Linji questioned Huangbo three times, receiving sixty blows of the black staff with no room for deliberation? On the banks of the Gao'an Rapids, he suddenly turned his body around.
He pulls back the tiger’s whiskers and delivers a painful slap; the practitioner abandons the teachings to come study Chan.

He risks my fist that would split his face, for he has personally obtained the *maṇi* jewel within the treasury. He must strike it to pieces before Mount Ouyang, then shake out his sleeves with dignity and walk out the gate.
On the roads of Jiangnan, the spring light is in full bloom; where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant. The phoenix does not dwell [in the cage].
The *wutong* tree: To serve as an attendant, a practitioner must learn to be like a fool.
Come and enter the chamber of the Foolish Hermit; the Foolish Hermit will teach you to be a fool. You have a mouth, yet you cannot speak it.
Neither spoken nor heard; neither gained nor lost. Shaking his head, he wanders through all directions; leaning on his staff, he picks up the red sun.
He laughs at old Xianglin, whose paper robe is black as lacquer. Three times three is not nine; nine times nine is eighty-one.
Seeing Elder Jian Return to Baosheng:
Do you not see how Jia Shan, upon dispersing his assembly, encountered Chuanzi? With a single pole, he struck him down into the blue waves;
his dead eyes suddenly opened wide, and he nodded his head. Only then did we know that my laughter had good reason. And do you not see Huanglong’s travels on foot?
Upon meeting Ciming, he was unable to restrain his bitter scolding, and his soul and gall were struck with alarm.

Only when he stepped upon the pivot of Zhaozhou’s barrier did he realize that Yunfeng’s utterances were beyond the ordinary. Lately, who can raise this story? Discourses on the wondrous and talk of the profound fill the world.
If one examines this from the perspective of the Zen monastic tradition, even at the end of the path, one dares not grant it lightly.
Now that you have attained the seat and donned the robes, what is the point of searching east and west? You have already turned back before even stepping onto the ship’s railing;

the vast earth is devoid of a true master. I recall our travels together were no mere day or two; we could laugh and talk while naturally forgetting gain and loss. Truly, you must have seen this for yourself.
The author arrives. The matters of your lifelong study are now complete. We shall part again tomorrow morning; a future meeting cannot yet be foreseen.
To send you back, I have one more word: when you return to your old mountain, do not fail to be heedful. When traveling at dawn, you must wait for the red sun to rise;
do not let the frost and dew moisten your hempen robes.

Sent forth to travel throughout all quarters, what is the ultimate purpose of this Zen practitioner? If you truly wish to investigate and clarify the matter of life and death, you must let go of everything from before.
Please, cast aside your black staff and try sitting quietly in an empty hall; suddenly, the beans will burst.
Cold ashes. It pains my mouth, yet it does not hinder me from reviling you.
Since I am utterly devoid of shame, I remain as if deaf and mute, laughing at how, in days of yore, Muzhou squeezed Yunmen until his feet were lame.
I present this to the Elder Abbot Xun as he sits in meditation upon his bed of withered wood; his mind has entered the wondrous samādhi beyond words.

A Chan practitioner from the mountain’s shade comes to knock at the gate, unrolling a cloud-patterned scroll to seek a long verse. Though I wish to write the long verse, I cannot finish it; I strike the inkstone with an iron whip until it shatters.
The *nirvāṇa*-pearl cannot be contained within the Tathāgatagarbha; its divine light shines brightly, soaring through the cold void.
It startles the white-foreheaded tiger of the South Mountain, while the wooden man claps his boards and dances in mid-air. In both the East and the West, there are no patriarchs;
five times five remains, as it always has, twenty-five.
To the Chan Master Xian, a man of the Way:
his backbone is forged of iron; he drags his staff across the earth with eyes like those of a hawk.

He has wandered through the forests seeking out masters of wisdom, opening his mouth as if to swallow the Buddhas of the three ages. Upon the back of the golden tortoise, he turns his body around, laughing as he points toward the heights of Lingxiao Peak.
Stark and abrupt! Having secured the pearl within the Tathāgatagarbha, one casually brushes past the lair of the azure dragon.
Two fellow practitioners passed by and conversed with me at night. One friend said, "This matter is most difficult; it cannot be grasped through deliberation.
The other friend said, "This matter is most easy; it is simply that one cannot take responsibility for it oneself."
Listen! I shall therefore illustrate this with two primary difficulties that encompass ten thousand kinds and a thousand variations.
The moment you attempt to deliberate, you are already muddled and coarse. It is like a thunderclap in the clear blue sky, or waves surging across level ground.
Non-explanation is the true explanation; other views are not correct contemplation. One may sink into delusion and waste vast eons, yet awakening lies within the tip of a hair.
Do not let yourself sit idly in the Han-yuan Palace, merely seeking Chang’an whenever you meet someone.

Extremely easy, with manifold approaches converging into one. Transcending all reception and forgetting all metaphors, it shines through antiquity and soars through the present; it spans the heavens and weaves the earth.
Whether known or unknown, benefiting others is itself self-benefit. This is the luminous True Vehicle of Prajñā, yet in every thought-moment there are the affairs of worldly toil.
Uproot the roots of the bitter gourd of many years; Śākyamuni did not receive the prediction from Dīpaṃkara.

The *maṇi* within the treasury of Preceptor Fan is unrecognized by men; It was personally retrieved upon the banks of the River Dragon. Now brought forth before Mount Ou, a single divine radiance pierces the azure void.
Placed in turbid water, the turbid water becomes clear; When the mountain ghosts behold it, their souls are startled.

My heart leaps with alarm; I wish to snatch it back from him immediately. To cast it away for the sake of illuminating the dark paths of the world—Yangshan emptied out his wicker basket, leaving the forest in disarray;
this is no small matter. You now cherish it as a supreme treasure, but in the end, why not simply let it go?
Da’an’s words have nothing to rely upon; you may as well take them with you back to Jinling. As the occasion demands.
Manifesting both form and non-form—the old barbarian’s two eyes remain crystalline and bright.
Huìsòng succeeded Wéinà, and Cuìyán received Yunfēng; Kèbīn inherited Xùnhuà. The transmission between master and disciple was by no means trivial. For a thousand ages, the monastic assembly...
Línchéng speaks: The man of the Way wishes to follow in the footsteps of the former sages; He has specially cleared away the brambles to come and join me.

In the battle of Dharma, there is no need to debate victory or defeat; The goal of passing the examination at the patriarchal altar is the realization of an empty mind. I now bind my hut upon the summit of a solitary peak; For many years, my consciousness has been like cold ashes.
I am too weary to wield the staff or shout the *kan* and *hat* at others; I gaze upward at the blue sky and the silent bright sun.
The Way-man again traveled through various regions, earnestly requesting that I raise the *huatou*. When the *huatou* is raised, it is simply this:
in the Great Peace, what need is there for the application of spears and halberds?
Presented to Chan Master Chong, with deep sighs and yet more sighs: Who can discern the pivotal point of the ultimate state?

There are many who occupy the high seat of the *ruyuluo* (curved bench), yet what benefit is there in merely echoing sounds and grasping at emptiness? Do you not see that at Tiger Hill, it was none other than Master Long who stood uniquely upon the patriarchal altar?
His reputation is widespread. O Chan Master Chong, O Chan Master Chong! You who soar high in the Great Way must exert yourself.
The mists and clouds have aged me; my heart is as cold ash. I wish only to behold the ancient splendor of the monastic groves.

Master Qizang seeks the pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ crowns; transcending all measures and limits, he penetrates the passageway that reaches through the heavens—only then is what he has attained truly authentic.
The practitioner was in the prime of his years; having resolved to strive upward, he took up his staff and carried his bowl and bag to travel east and west in search of instruction.
Ascending once more to Mount Lingxiao, he admired the example of the ancients; his conduct remained refined and strict, and the friends he made were no ordinary or frivolous men.
Coming and going, or not coming and going; this treasury, or not this treasury—how very clear it is before one’s eyes! Yet opening one’s mouth turns it into slander.
Do not listen to Master Du, whose secret words are but flattery and deception. Return home and examine it with care; there is another extraordinary aspect.
Master Heng, as you escort [the guest], hold fast at the pivot of the profound mystery; let not even a drop of water leak through. As for that one step beyond—how is it to be discerned?

Even if one’s discernment flows like a river and one’s wit strikes like a flash of lightning, upon reaching this point, one must still cast off armor and overturn the spearhead, losing all edge and rendering the tongue mute. To speak... *Note: The final character "說" (shuō) appears to be an incomplete sentence marker or a prompt for further discourse.*
What is this of staff and shout exchanged, striking and singing in perfect harmony? Thus it is said: "The golden-haired lion crouches on the ground, exerting its full majesty;
when the jackal hears it, its brain splits open. Yet, as for Linji’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, why did it instead perish within the blind donkey?
Although there is host and guest, in the end there is neither demonstration nor explanation. Constantly meditating, constantly meditating—do you understand?
I do not know. What time was it in the past? What time is it now? The melodic strain of Shaolin is naturally distinct;
even Huang Jin could not cast a bell for Zichqi.
In this rhyme, I bid farewell to the Abbot Zhen of Lingyin.
The majestic body of Vairocana is revealed in full splendor; from antiquity to the present, there has been no discrepancy.

Upon the tip of a single hair, the source is thoroughly penetrated, like the sun traversing the sky at its zenith. Recalling the Great Master Ma of Jiangxi, whose fame and brilliance blazed across the earth—truly, his manner of exhortation was unique;
observe how he wielded the staff and let out the shout. O clever patch-robed monks!
Quickly you must provide proof; you may not remain silent, nor may you utter a word. Turn over and root out the thicket of entanglements in the Tripitaka;
even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot restrain you. Startle the sleeping lynx from within the grass; bite to death the white-marked tiger of the Southern Mountains.
Before the Master of the Tripitaka, Dharma, arrived from the West, everyone’s nostrils pointed toward heaven; the Buddha of True Nature was never obscured, manifesting in every aspect of daily life.
Yet, by the time he reached Liang and traveled through Wei, his bones were exposed and his skin worn through; even Shen Guang’s prostration was a mistake.
Three prostrations. From this point on, the flame shall continue and the fragrant lineage be linked. Linji has no further basis; he merely passed down a single shout.

Who would have known that the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was extinguished within the reach of this blind donkey? Old as I am, white mold grows upon my lips; how could I find the leisure to preach Chan for others?
Tomorrow I shall return to Dongting; it will not hinder me to sail with the current.
To the Abbot Zong on the Matter Beyond the Zen Gate: There is no transmission and no reception; This paper robe was obtained by copying. I cannot help but expose my family’s disgrace.
An old man atop Five Peaks, Too lazy to open my mouth for others. Whenever I encounter a disciple entering the room, I strike them across the spine with a great mallet.

Although one need not differentiate according to individual capacities, what is prized is liberation from the old molds. If you are a person of brilliant spirit, you ought to know that there is something prior to the functioning of the mind.

The teachings of the Tripitaka number over five thousand scrolls and have been disseminated for a very long time; yet to overturn them all to the very bottom is no small feat—it is enough to boast of being a master of the craft.
The old Yunmen was thoroughly scrutinized; in a single stroke, forty-nine blows were dealt.

To the guest prefect Zhi, at the place where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it. Before the trigger is pulled, he has pierced through the patriarch’s barrier; both saintly understanding and worldly sentiment are exhausted.
Set it aside! Have you not seen how at Dayang Monastery, Guest Master Xian made the bystander Han Dabe laugh until he fell over?
Perched high upon the lion throne at the peak of Nanyue, his fame has blazed forth for a thousand ages.
The master of the treasury, Ze, sends [this] from Mount Guangzang.
A principle capable of subduing a leopard allows sentient beings to forever cease their攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to conditions). The Buddhas originally possess no verbal teachings;
Zhaozhou’s turning of the Tripitaka for the old woman was far too coarse and reckless. Yet, it did not hinder Shanhui from lecturing on the sutras before Emperor Liang.
Selling the steep precipice: you should know that wherever you touch, you encounter the source. Be most careful not to lose your illumination by merely following circumstances.

A man of the Way studies the art of "empty liberation," seeking wholeheartedly for real efficacy. Having visited me at the summit of Lingxiao Peak, he steps upon the aperture that pierces through to heaven. Grasping his black staff upside down, he turns his body about;
beyond the mundane world, he wanders freely, exulting in his lofty stride.

Sending off Abbot Xiu, he passes through the Red-Tailed Carp Gate of Longmen. With a flip, the waves and billows rise from the sea; his momentum to seize the clouds and snatch the mist shows no sign of ceasing.
In the end, he will never be submerged within a jar of minced vegetables. At this old monk’s place of stillness, *svāhā*. All day long, my two eyes remain suspended.

Pines and lichens: when autumn enters the groves, they are in full decay. Who can moisten and nourish them by pouring down the Milky Way? The transformations of fish and dragons are indeed unfathomable;
you, O Master, should exert yourself on this journey. Baizhang went back to study under Mazu Daoshi; it is said he once heard a single shout that deafened him for three days.
In memory of Chan Master Nian, a sincere seeker of the Way: His backbone is as hard as iron; right mindfulness is ever-present before him. The profound pivot is thoroughly penetrated;
he raises the rhinoceros fan. A pure breeze stirs the vast void; he opens wide the inexhaustible treasury. The dragon pearl shines like the bright moon.
Turning his head, he returns; he does not fall into the tracks of others. A lion cub emerging from the forest, his natural prowess is extraordinary.
Like the attendant Ruru, he enters directly and immediately into the gate of the Tathāgata’s sudden teaching. He severs the root of intellectual views and sheds the attachments of emotional dust.

The "sucking" and "pecking" occur at the very moment of action; how could they be anything less than swift as a split arrow? Not for a moment does one rely on deliberation—how could anyone say there are gradual stages involved?
When Baizhang attended Mazu, he stood to the side by the meditation platform; when the master suddenly seized him with his whisk, Baizhang covered his ears, but in the end it was too late.
Turning iron into refined gold—a single grain of the elixir of immortality.
When Mazu ascended the hall, Baizhang rolled up his mat; the Great Function was fully revealed, its divine mechanism unfathomable, like a magnet attracting a needle.
Like an arrowhead piercing its target, father and son have transmitted and upheld this; fundamentally, there is nothing mysterious or secret about it.

You, Yuan Chan, have come into my room, leaping out of the tangles of conceptual entanglement and crashing against the iron wall. A hot shout and a true punch—like thunder crashing and lightning flashing. To conceive of it with the mind is already to deviate from it.
To open one’s mouth is to lose it; to tear asunder the past and present is indeed extraordinary, yet it is like pulling a tiger’s whiskers—fit only for a thief who steals in broad daylight.

When the attendant Bai sent Jing to Master Niaoke, the latter blew upon some cloth-hair, and the attendant attained enlightenment immediately. This was a meeting of minds like a mustard seed rolling into a needle’s eye; to boast of "the arrowhead meeting the arrowhead" is merely empty vainglory.
The sun rises high in the heavens; the clouds disperse and the mountains are revealed. Bright and clear, there is no concealment; distinct and lucid, there is no turning back.
Having forced one's way through the ultimate barrier, one treads the path by which they came. As for the "Four Sevens" and the "Two Threes," their secret intent was never transmitted.

The first phrase and the final word for the tree-guardian Sangzhu: before opening one’s mouth, one knows where it lands. When Niaoke picked up a tuft of cloth and blew upon it, the attendant Huitong immediately attained awakening.
Thus, the Buddha’s teaching and the Patriarchs’ Chan are entirely devoid of secret meanings fit for transmission.
The daily activities of life are clear and manifest; the numinous light penetrates through to before the time of Weiyin.

The entire Great Canon of Teachings is spoken as one—how can even a monk with clear eyes discern it? The Persian from the South Sea smiles and raises his brows; behind the diamond-hard skull is three catties of iron.
Attendant Chan Master Hanseng has attained realization through Zen; with a thousand ends and a hundred beginnings, he turns his body toward that further shore.

Having pierced through the Tathāgatagarbha, he extracts the *maṇi* jewel from within; its brilliant radiance blazes forth, pervading the ten directions, such that neither sage nor ordinary person can approach it.
Beside it, Śakra’s eye cannot peer; as soon as this old monk sees it, he snatches it away. He suddenly questions him from the beginning, demanding it back.
Walking together through the weeds for no reason, the Great Elder of the Eastern Village laughs himself to tears.
*Ei-hu-xi*—no one knows! Holding his iron flute crosswise, he blows into the wind. The Ten-Shadow Divine Steed stands on the shore of the sea; the Nine-Clawed Auspicious Phoenix...
Soaring into the void, he sent the Abbot Zuncang to the state where there is nothing to realize;
he reached the stage where there is nothing more to learn. The teacherless wisdom suddenly manifested before him, and both sacred understanding and mundane sentiment were utterly exhausted.
Set it aside! The entire Tripitaka is merely a foot-note. Dongshan explained *pātra* as *nāga*; the Sanskrit term does not encompass the meaning of the Chinese.
A man of the Way has recently come from Yunfeng; his aspiration to explore the profound is extraordinary.
He has severed the web of former views and knowledge; with one leap through the Dragon Gate, he stirs wind and thunder. His rabbit-horn staff is lively and agile—strike!
Seizing whatever one pleases from the void—do not boast of Linji’s mere page-boy. Huangbo once stroked the tiger’s whiskers backward.
To the Librarian Qizang:
Opening wide the heavy gates to invite a great adversary, he casually seizes the white-handed thief; the trident of the Three Mysteries is needlessly deployed.
Presented. When biting the arrowhead, one must discern the point of engagement. It is laughable that Wenyuan and Zhaozhou contended with their lips and tongues for no reason at all.
They sought only to compete in inferiority rather than victory; how could they know they had become enemies, father and son?

How much better it would be to enter deeply into the Vairocana-realm, where neither saint nor ordinary person can approach. Grasping the universe, the true command is executed—eminent beyond antiquity.
Now, this is the true model. At times, he wields mastery and lets go, exerting his full majesty; with a single roar, he is a lion cub.
The Vajra emerges from its sheath, blazing with radiant flames; how could the Śakara eye possibly gaze upon it?
Seeing off Chief Seat Xian as he returns to receive the scriptures:

The clouds across the eight directions are pure, the autumn air is lofty; A breeze rises from the cassia peaks, and the fragrance of heaven drifts forth. The head monk in the hall has just arisen from meditation;
Rolling up his robes, he intends to cross the tides of the Dragon River. Though entreated again and again, he refuses to stay; With iron staff slung over his shoulder, he departs.
The gate has closed; he shall return another day to stroke the tiger’s whiskers. The "sipping" and "pecking" strike the pivot like the point of an arrow meeting its shaft.
The single melody of Shaolin is difficult for listeners to hear; who now plays the zither without strings? I, an old man, lean against the courtyard tree reaching toward the clouds;
rubbing my two eyes, I watch the Peng bird soar.
Song for the "Reclining Amidst Clouds" Pavilion, written for Chan Master Dajī of Water West:

For one who dwells within the "Reclining Amidst Clouds" Pavilion, Mundane affairs do not reach him; his mind is as leisurely as the clouds. He gazes upon the clouds, casually entrusting his pride to them.
That clouds follow dragons can surely be expected; that a man of great attainment responds to the world must have its proper time.

Thus one knows that expansion and contraction are fundamentally traceless, as the vast expanse of the six directions follows wherever it may go. I earnestly inform you, O recluse who lies amidst the clouds:
there is a path within the clouds upon which you must set foot. The people of this great earth look toward the rain; why do you remain long reclined by the shores of the southern lake?

**Song of Beyond Emptiness (with Preface)** The Abbot of Donglin, Shicang, whose style name is Kongwai (Beyond Emptiness), requested that I compose a verse to corroborate his teaching. I therefore said to him:
"Emptiness has neither interior nor exterior; the nature of both interior and exterior is empty. Even this emptiness of nature is itself empty. Within ultimate emptiness, there is no name."
"The characteristics of letters are devoid of the characteristics of verbal expression. Your establishment of names is very much like attempting to clip and cut through empty space.

I shall further speak a verse; how is this any different from painting pictures upon empty space? Sengshi said, "I have established the name 'emptiness,' and you, Master, have spoken verses on emptiness.
To receive emptiness with emptiness—is this not permissible? "I never expected that within the boundaries of Mount Lu there would be such a man of empty talk."
It is so. Striking the meditation board, he sang this song:

"The true nature is equal to empty space; vast and penetrating, it has neither interior nor exterior. It is neither identical with nor separate from [phenomena]; it is neither facing toward nor turning away."
If a person can, in a single thought-moment, achieve thorough integration, then every head and every object reveals the True Principle. The ten directions are vast and boundless;
from antiquity to the present, essence and function are one. Whether identical or not, different or not, there is no real meaning in talk of "beyond emptiness.
A single stroke of the mechanism transcends the era of Wei-yin; even the Śūnyatā-deva treads upon the ground. Sometimes it comes from beyond emptiness.
The head is as steep as the Five Peaks, towering and majestic; the layered, inexhaustible Flower Treasury Worlds are each opened wide from the very beginning.
Sometimes he goes beyond the void; even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands cannot restrain him. Turning his body, he kicks over the Seven Golden Mountains.
Every land and every mote of dust is the path of return. A-he-he! Do you understand?
When I sing this song of empty liberation in the midst of the sun, who can do anything to hinder my joy? The stone man by the stream whispers to one another; a featherless iron hawk flies to Silla.

In the great function, one who sings the song of selecting the Buddha attains the highest rank; throughout antiquity and the present, who can rival this? The great function is ever manifest before us—why need one preserve formal rules?
To pluck the bright pearl from beneath the jaw of the black dragon, to bare-handedly comb the whiskers of a fierce tiger, and to turn over the vertebrae upon the back of empty space.

A *dou* measure. Dwelling together within the pores of a lotus fiber; seizing the white-handed thief before the pivot of action. Pressing straight and lifting from the side—people do not recognize it.
Hanging a sword between the brows is truly extraordinary. Penetrating the golden circle and swallowing the thorny chestnut.
Behold the heavenly spirit’s vigor and his wind-like elegance as he ascends directly to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, rolling Mount Sumeru out like a brocade ball. Suddenly—
Passing through worlds beyond counting in other directions, he turns his body and brings it toward my heels and head.
A-he-he! Is it good or not? North, south, east, west—where can one seek it? Upon the tip of a single hair, one recognizes the source; both the holy and the ordinary are cast down together.
Having recently encountered this great function, you demand my song of the Great Function. I am ashamed of my own meager talent and strength, yet how can I refuse you, O Great One?
What is used? Try taking a single drop of Caoxi’s water to swell the vast, boundless waves of the Western River.
Its ripples coldly soak the azure lapis lazuli; it drenches the sun and floods the heavens, its depth unfathomable.
To drink it dry with a single breath takes not the slightest effort. Know this and cease your alarm and doubt: for the monk who seeks the ultimate, there is yet further instruction to be upheld.
Brightness cast upon darkness, meeting in perfect integration; total release, turning left and circling right, neither identical nor separate.
The Great Space fills both within and without; its wondrous function, whether horizontal or vertical, is inexhaustible.
The Song of Daiman (with Preface) I have maintained myself through my own dullness and stupidity.
Wherever I dwell, I have inscribed the name "Dai-an" (The Dull Hermitage). A guest once remarked in derision:
"For a long time now, the people of the world have vied with one another in cleverness and ingenuity. You wish to preserve your dullness and correct them; is this not perverse?"
This is also rather circuitous. I therefore took leave of my guest, saying, "Only a clever fellow would make such distinctions.
Once the guest had departed, I composed this "Song of the Dullard" to express the sentiments of one who is dull. Those who read it should not judge it by its literary skill or lack thereof.
I am this Daoist of Daiman (Stupid Hermitage), who knows nothing of autumn or spring in this world. I pass my days in a state of dazed and foolish stillness;
there is no honor, no disgrace, no distance, and no intimacy. Sometimes I sell fine gold mixed with earth; sometimes I collect common "swallow stones" and treasure them as jewels.
This makes the clever onlookers laugh until they fall over; yet I feel no joy when praised and no anger when reviled. If anyone asks about Daiman:
What is there to do? Idly watching a gourd hanging in a corner by the wall, I pick up a blunt iron spade right before my eyes.
I intend to go and dig into empty space; yet the gate has stood wide open for years, and the interior has always been utterly bare.

Often one is deceived right in the face by the worldly crowd, remaining oblivious to this throughout a whole life of blundering confusion. How strange that such a dull-witted person can accomplish nothing! Facing [the world]...
A person who is dull-witted is already loathsome; now he speaks of the night being deep and the straw dogs barking. A man picks up a lamp at the bottom of the great ocean.
Yet there is another sort of dull-witted trickery: his two ears stick out and his hair is disheveled.
No matter how much you, O guest-monk, display your cleverness, calling him from the east and the west, he does not respond.
A Song for Wuyan (with Preface).
The Abbot Wuyan of Yue requested that I compose a song based on his name. Although I repeatedly declined, his entreaty remained steadfast.
He then said to him, "I have been composing this song for a long time; it is simply that you have not heard it.
Yue replied, "Since the Master speaks without speaking, he must also speak of that which is beyond speech. How could there be any further discrimination?
I smiled and, taking up my brush, wrote a verse to satisfy his request.
The Venerable Wuyan requested a song from me; I was precisely in the state of wordlessness, delighting in the stillness of Chan.
Utterly unmoving, I sat there without answering, a massive heap of presence, my two eyes staring blankly at the empty wall. After a long while, the Venerable left the room.
Who could discuss this matter clearly? The sun hung high and bright at the meridian; the pine wind whistled, its sound filling the hall. Vimalakīrti manifested illness.
In Vaiśālī, it was only fitting that Mañjuśrī should arrive; yet once he arrived, he never uttered a single word.
The Gate of Non-duality opened with world-shaking brilliance: "Now you hear nothing and I say nothing. Face-to-face, seizing the opportune moment, it is direct and immediate.
The True Man of No-Rank smiles with an open countenance, while Koṭikarṇa gasps in astonishment and sticks out his tongue.
Song of the Cloud Sea. Composed for the Master Cizang.
The compassionate clouds provide shade and cover, vast and boundless; The ocean of awakening is perfectly clear and deep, unfathomable. It all comes down to a single hair-tip;
Cast before one's eyes, yet people do not recognize it. Let it cast its reflections throughout the ten directions, Constantly sprinkling nectar to revive all beings.
Scorched and withered, it encompasses the trichiliocosm; ten billion Mount Sumerus emerge from it. Contemplate this ocean of clouds thoroughly, from its source to its end;
from antiquity to the present, it is beyond compare. Turn over the very bottom to test the master; a mere blink of the eyebrows separates one by a thousand miles.
The Master above requests from me a song of the ocean of clouds; I sing of the ocean of clouds—what can be done? It has not yet opened.

The sound of his voice was vast and resonant; like the Dragon Gate drumming up waves that overflow the heavens, he sang of the "Jing-shi" at Mount Jing-shan—therein lies a stone, solitary and magnificent.
Who knows it to be a flawless jade gem? When Bian He beheld it once, he rejoiced.
Startled! I hold it forth to present at the Golden Gate, attempting to refine its form. Such master craftsmen of the state of Chu are rare, indeed rare.
Alas, he returned from Mount Jing with his stones in his arms; one day, through decisive action, he met a wise sovereign. This Heaven-born supreme treasure is truly peerless.
I have recently heard that Mount Jing still abounds in common stones—how could there be a "city-connecting" jade among them? Cowherds cast them aside like tiles and rubble; the age lacks a Bianshi.

Who in this world can truly recognize it? Every practitioner of the Way harbors a priceless treasure within themselves. Since the Master-Craftsman has long ceased his work, these treasures remain buried in dust.
Whether they are buried or not, what loss or gain is there? The day will surely come when they respond to conditions to benefit all beings.

I pray that from now on you will protect and uphold this well; do not give way to despondency along the way. A practitioner requested a song for me regarding the thorn-tree stone, which I have here recorded.
The song continues with sighs: "What can be done? The jade from the Jing River longs for its home; do not sell it lightly. Throughout the ages, slander has always been rife.

I chant my verses on the joy of *dhyāna*; who can bear witness to this joy of *dhyāna*? Only those with true discernment know the place of bliss. Lightly rolling up my *kāṣāya*, I emerge from the dust of the world.
Come! Shouldering my staff high, I enter the mountains. Beneath the green pines and before the azure cliffs, I idly watch the floating clouds stretching across the dawn sky.
As the sun’s orb first rises to illuminate the summit, the great earth in an instant becomes entirely radiant.

At the Stone Gate Hermitage, along the path of wild grass, I go when I wish to go and stay when I wish to stay. Sometimes I sit motionless upon my worn wooden bench; when weary, I stretch out with my robes still on.
Sleeping on one's feet; this poor mendicant has no intimates or kin. In every application, all is the true nature of heaven. A mountain bird suddenly passes by, carrying a flower;
returning from meditation, he does not realize that spring has come to the human world. All phenomena are empty, myriad conditions severed; the *campaka* blows its fragrance through the vast void.
Having finished reading the *Laṅkāvatāra*, he remains silent and speechless; raising his head, he gazes afar at the moon at the edge of the sky. Autumn leaves fall in autumn.
The breeze is cool; the sound of the flowing mountain stream is naturally long. At twilight, I unexpectedly encounter a woodcutter.
As I seek the path home, why do I linger? Alone, I sigh with constant joy and delight; I have severed a thousand demons and a hundred monsters.

Throughout the deep winter, accumulated snow covers the mountains and forests—far surpassing the silver world of Samantabhadra. It cannot be depicted nor can it be painted; I have realized the state of non-arising.
There is nothing that does not arise. One bowl brought the fragrant food of the Accumulated Fragrance; Vimalakīrti did not leave the city of Vaiśālī. The joy of dhyāna is inexhaustible;
the functional application of a true monk is distinct. At this very moment of total release and total gathering, I send word to those of penetrating understanding:
examine and discern well!
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Six;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Seven.
Compiled by his junior disciples Tandong and others.
Poem (Heptasyllabic Verse, Eight Lines):

For over thirty years, I have read the Recorded Sayings of Master Gulin, who revitalized the ancestral wind. This Chan master’s approach was not like others; his eye for testing people was located right between his eyebrows.
Above. The tiger-trapping mechanism is held within the palm; from withered wood, branches sprout, hanging green to the ground;
from cold ashes, flames burst forth, stretching red across the heavens. Behold him shatter the浑侨 (hún lón) phrase and sweep past Yangqi’s thorny chestnut burr.

I send Master Jian, the Abbot of Yangshan, to seek teachers and choose companions for the study of Chan. To practice Chan, one must be as firm as iron and stone; to gaze toward the wind from a thousand miles away is ultimately in vain.
Only when one lets out a sudden cry of realization will joy truly arise. When the snow melts at Mount Yuling, the spring staff flies forth; when the moon fills the Poyang River, the night deepens.
Plying the boat, he plucks the "black pearl" with its brilliant luster; atop the peak of Cloud-Gathering Mountain, the waves overflow the heavens.
Sending off Attendant Min (who was then at Beichan Temple in Fuzhou):

"Wading through the grass and observing the wind, you did not shrink from toil; yet most of your time was spent in idle neglect. At this very moment, it is precisely when one should exercise the Three [Secrets].
Sudden! On level ground, one must still beware of tripping. The yellow wagtails compete to peck at the red rice; the purple pheasants incline toward nesting in the green wutong trees.
Beichan has words that are not merely idle chatter; do not trouble the attendant to transcribe this paper robe.
Sent to Attendant Ziyao:

To travel through the various quarters, one must recognize the Real. These words and this practice should be inscribed upon your girdle. Chasing after sounds and pursuing forms, it is difficult to escape the dust of the world;
severing thoughts and forgetting conditions, the Way is easily approached. Though all say there is cultivation and realization, you must know that even the "Dharma-less" is not to be grasped.
No person. A wisp of cloth-buffalo hair rises, and the twin pupils are azure; the flower blooms at the tip of the pestle, a spring beyond the kalpas.
(In the same rhyme: Sending off Attendant Jie to Xiangxi.
In the past, Attendant Kuò’s decisive shout startled his contemporaries; he broke free from all snares and soared toward the heavens.

The falcon forgets both whip and tether—this is the ox in the open field; the arrow is set and the bow drawn—this is the thought of Shigong. Displaying the oar and dancing with the paddle, one laughs at Yantou.
To the east of Fusang, the misty waves are vast; there will surely come a Kun or a Jie to ascend the straight hook.
I bid farewell to Chan Master Zangzhu:
you who study the Way, do not linger. Cold and heat hasten one toward gray hair.

Since you have set out on foot to know the Great Matter, you must resolve to continue the practice of those who came before. To understand Linji’s visit to Huangbo, you must contemplate Yunmen’s meeting with...
Muzhou: With a casual hand, he overturns the ocean of the Flower Treasury Sūtra; he roams at will upon the back of empty space.
To Master Quanshi:
Having retired to live in leisure by the imperial capital in my old age, I have received imperial favor and once again served the majesty of Heaven. The intent of the Three Sutras.

The secret instructions were once presented to the Emperor; the true transmission of the thousand sages was fully revealed. Su Shi received the Buddha’s seal upon his girdle; Daian left behind the robe of Han Yu.
Court scholars inquired about the Dharma as frequently as falling rain; each and every one was guided by the upward-tending pivot.
Attendant Yan presented a verse to the Master. The Master composed two verses in response, matching its rhyme:

Carrying his iron-tipped staff across my shoulder, I have traveled far from the capital to this forest retreat. I shall bring forth the vast clarity that illuminates the eyes of gods and men, and investigate the ultimate mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Who says it is difficult to fashion a mirror by grinding tiles? I know how to transform iron into gold.
Ordinary metal is easily transformed into gold; when the faculty of discernment recognizes it, one returns to the source.
A zither without strings produces wondrous music; the patriarchs’ "head-words" are like iron spikes. These have been circulated through the ages, filling the monastic groves.
Do not strive to listen to my idle chatter; take care not to follow others with a mistaken mind. Jade becomes a beautiful vessel through polishing; ore yields its essence through smelting.
Refined gold! Lightly struck with the earthen drum of Mount Dongshan, it is none other than the thundering roar of empty space.
The profound secret intent of the venerable Elder Zongsheng is entirely within you;
I have no secret words to transmit to others. This is intended solely as a light for this degenerate age.

Do not study the "silent illumination" Chan of others. Let acceptance and rejection be entirely cast aside beyond the scope of the mind; let your conduct and concealment penetrate directly through the void before kalpas.
To enter the marketplace and extend a helping hand, one must employ skillful means; for now, the age of the Dharma’s decline has reached ten thousand years.

In the same rhyme. Sent to Attendant Qín: Beyond the skull-caps, there is a spiritual light; In daily life, it is ever-bright and never hidden. The Way transcends verbal explanation—reflect upon this yourself;
The timing of the "peck" and the "tap" must coincide. Do not vainly follow Luopu to leave Linji; Constantly contemplate Longhu to see [the truth].
Shishuang: "The forests of the four seas are now utterly desolate; who can, with bare hands, restore the collapsing order?
Following the rhyme of Master Xuefeng Kong’s *Fensui* (Distributing the Year), I write this while meeting the year at Jingshan:
Distributing the year with others, the family banquet has just begun; the fragrance of the soup boiled from wood chips fills the air."
The earth; the aroma of rice steaming over iron nails forms clouds. Thinly sliced, there are over a thousand pieces of the bright moon; finely minced, there are hundreds of catties of the pure wind.
Blown forth is the unperforated flute of Shaolin; no monk has ever heard such a thing before.
In the same rhyme, I respond to my Dharma-nephew, Master Zecang, regarding the matter of "before the birth of the Buddha.

The humble may be worthy of the lowly, and the noble may be worthy of the honorable; precisely when the path of speech has no place to be sought, one can truly believe that the Chan school possesses a gate of awakening.
With a single snap of the fingers, one directly causes the three periods of time to be severed; in the end, do not be caught by the six [senses].
The dust of the world is dimmed; had it not been for the visit of my Dharma-nephew, how could this old man have found words to discourse?

To bid farewell to Chan Master Bian upon his inquiry after my name, I shall offer only a single silence in response. Without moving the root of the tongue, discernment flows like a stream; yet if one attempts to seek the path of the profound, it is but empty winnowing.
With power, one penetrates to the true source and finally reaches the ultimate end. Wearing leather shoes, one treads upon the clouds as the two paths dawn;

carrying a wooden cup, one rides the moon over Lake Dongting in autumn. Bright and clear, the "lid covering the earth" phrase stands upright and sweeps across horizontally, attained with complete freedom.

As the Abbot Yuan sets out to travel among the various monasteries, his resolve is firm: "The heart-seal of the Patriarchs must be transmitted personally. How does his striking the meditation seat differ from his wondrous responses to guests?

His exchange with the monk, joined palms in reply, is already complete. The mountain paths of Jingwu are deep and secluded, clouds winding around the thatched roof; Lake Tai is vast and empty, its waters—
Reaching to the heavens. To fully know that every dharma is without differentiation—where, then, does this hidden intent reside?

Master Chizang, as you travel, let your conduct not be separate from the Way; throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, maintain it well. Suddenly stilling all conditions, there is no difference [from the Way].
The Path: As soon as a single thought arises, there are many diverging branches. How could this luminous clarity be sought from another?
Once clearly understood, why should it not be known by oneself? The mani-jewel within the treasury shines with brilliant light; when brought forth, it shatters the doubts of all people.
In the same rhyme: Presented to my Dharma nephew, Zen practitioner Ze.
Holding up the black, shaggy *kāṣāya*, you have been entrusted for many years to leave this hermitage. Since the ancestral Way has no one to transmit it, the responsibility falls upon me;
when there is talk in the Gate of the School, to whom can it be addressed? When Ciming took off his sandals before Shending, and Zhaojue struck the bell to receive [his successor].
Little Nan, today I grant you thirty blows. This present case requires no further investigation.

I bestow upon Abbot Yin the entire Tripitaka to be recited in a single breath. Turning the body and leaping out of the thicket of entanglements—coming and going in perfect accord—all proceeds from this.
I am one who kills or gives life according to the occasion, not subject to others. How many can truly be called men of measure? Those who possess the eye that transcends the mundane are likewise few.
Having traveled throughout Jiangnan and the two Zhe regions, I now hang my *kāṣāya* upon the *bìluó* vines.
In the same rhyme. Two poems in response to Master Bairyōng of Wanshou.

Sitting in a quiet room, wall-gazing, the *zuidu* [is silent]. How could speech or silence ever have traversed the marketplace? I simply hold the Patriarch’s seal before the mind’s movement; Let him keep his spiritual talisman hidden behind his elbow.
In the mirror, my hair and beard are a thousand strands of snow; At the corner of my bed, the rattan staff is seven... (Note: The final line of the second poem is incomplete in the source text.)
The Cheetah and the Crow: I only fear that the imperial summons will arrive from the heavens, and that you must hasten to court to receive the special gift of the golden robe.
I recall when we were together on Mount Baizhu, spreading the supreme lineage; our verses of praise were brilliantly radiant, and the manner of holding the bamboo staff was majestic and imposing.
Who says there is no one to join in the "Snow Song"? I am confident that within the profound gate, there is indeed [a response].
The road is open. Since our parting, I have heard early news that you have returned to your native village; students of Chan from all quarters are all following your lead.
Following the original rhyme, I respond to the Abbot Wuwen regarding his travels to seek teachers and choose friends:
he has shattered the knot of doubt and brought forth the light of wisdom; with a single phrase, he transmits the Dharma when the occasion arises.
Seal. For ten years I mingled my tracks within the meditation hall. The cold pines stand tall, their trunks reaching toward the heavens in elegance;
the autumn chrysanthemums hang their flowers, yellow with the dew. Wondrous function is manifested at every turn; one realizes that the secret treasury cannot be hidden.
Sent forth to serve as a library keeper, he sought the Master by observing the wind and parting the grass; having arrived at Longmen in person, he no longer harbored doubt.

Though it was up to me to strip him of his pride with all my might, who else could have brought about this total surrender? To know the place where names and models are cut off, one must believe that the karmic conditions are like the simultaneous act of spitting.
When pecking, whether it be you or me who bears the burden, do not ask at all. Behold the sleeping tiger exerting its full majesty.
Venerable Weina, you have come seeking a verse;
what would you do with it? Go forth to various quarters and knock at the doors of veteran masters; within their words, they conceal the sharp point—therein you must be fierce.

A word of caution: Biting the arrowhead before the trigger is pulled—do not hesitate. You should know that the moment of direct, face-to-face guidance is precisely the time when one lets go of the whole body.
I did not follow Xinghua’s command; my parting instructions at the crossroads were but a waste of words.
When the attendant Shi-jian asked for instruction, the attendant had already attained Zen; thirty blows of the black staff were not lightly spared.

This fully causes the mental machinations of the patch-robed disciples to cease, thereby manifesting the high skillful means of the master. A mirror reflects light only when polished repeatedly; gold is revealed from its ore through a hundred refinements.
All has been dissolved. How limitless is the succession of empty echoes? To mend the broken thread, one must surely boil phoenix glue.
Poem (Heptasyllabic Quatrain):
In Response to Master Jiashì’s Four Miscellaneous Verses.
Sunk in emptiness and stalled in stillness, they do not turn back; as heat departs and cold arrives, spring follows autumn. The old bearded barbarian with missing teeth left the land of Zhuguo;
those of Mahayana capacity emerged from Shenzhou.
Seated, he cuts off the very peak of the solitary mountain; Deshan’s majestic bearing is as chilling as a high autumn.
Where his single white staff is wielded horizontally, his awesome prestige pervades the four hundred prefectures for a thousand ages.
In an empty study, silent, I scratch my head alone; I look out in alarm at the falling leaves, sensing the autumn of Jue Garden.
Though you presented ten thousand words upon which the Son of Heaven rejoiced, it makes me painfully miss you, old man of Tengzhou.
North of the river and south of the river, people race one another to the front; how many realize autumn has come when the leaves fall?
In his day, Fengxue took leave of Nanyuan; for seven years he lived alone in Ruizhou.
In the same rhyme as the Reverend of Dongyuan on Leisurely Dwelling:

Why must one go forth to receive guests when not descending from the hall? When host and guest are in accord, it is precious that worldly feelings are forgotten. The lofty style of Zhaozhou endures through the ages;
Without leaving the mountain gate, he beheld the King of Zhao.
I paid my respects at the ancestral stupa of Master Shushan and stole a listen to Dongshan’s Chan at the third watch. Father and son have never transmitted their wondrous secret;
having sold his cotton robe, for what reason did he remain until now, buried alive by the side of the great river?
Showing the monks how to build a bridge, the momentum of his hard-won effort does not cease; one must see that砥柱 (Dizhu) pillar standing firm in the middle of the stream.
Carrying donkeys and carrying horses are exactly the same—this makes one laugh at Old Zhaozhou of those days.
Title: Riding Backwards on the Ox The water-buffalo comes purely, never needing the whip. The vast plains stretch out, the grasses lush and green. Casually mounting it backwards, he steps forth;
A single horizontal flute-call pierces high into the heavens.

When Master Wen shows that there is no pointing-out at the time of pointing-out, and that there is no place for seeking when there is no seeking, it is essential to clarify what occurred prior to the birth of Buddhas;
one must bring to rest all various minds of restless pursuit.
I send this note to Secretary Zhong:
you have not yet wet your brush, yet your literary brilliance is revealed; I have barely opened my mouth, and my tongue has gone numb.
Last night, empty space laughed aloud "he-he," and the myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos together raised it on high.
I tell you, attendant:
in my school there are no words and no dharmas. Why are you so busy copying out these paper robes?
You must contemplate with cold detachment the single phrase: "Before your parents were born."
Presented to the Venerable Master Jiashì, Two Poems This matter of longing for home is unbearable;
In dreams and soul, I constantly wander around Lùluó Ān. An old recluse with white hair amidst the empty mountains— Who can be known as the one who attended his night-time discourse?
Carrying a seven-footed ancient rattan staff in hand, crossing waters and piercing through clouds—who could have foreseen it?
Neither traversing the path of adversity nor that of favor, I clearly explain this for the old Chan master to know.
Three Verses Sent to My Dharma Brother Xuánjí In his character, he did not spare even two strands of brow-hair; He personally encountered the ancient master [Zhǎo] of Mount Ān.
Now that the lineage pillar of Shaoshi has fallen to the ground, May those with strength in their wrists come forward to support it.
The old man at dusk holds a broken fishing line; once he bound the Qilin from the Eastern Sea.
Today he casts fragrant bait upon his long pole—how many can pull up the Golden Turtle?
A three-legged donkey gives birth to a wide-horned ox; it gallops and butts about east and west, leaving no trace of its path. It goes off to sleep soundly on the open ground;
since there is no rope through its nostrils, there is no need to tether it.
Two Poems on Shi Tantu showing his parents his filial piety:
When Niaoke picked up a tuft of cloth-hair and blew upon it, It was much like an empty fist deceiving a small child. Do not follow such deluded and inverted thoughts;
This old monk has no Dharma to transmit or uphold.
What parental affection can ever equal this? Folding my clothes, I bid you farewell with several tears. When you reach home, do not betray our promise to return to the mountains;
you must carry that broken-legged cauldron.
Sending off a practitioner of dhyāna:
the gates of the wise are as deep as the sea. Pack light and take a short staff; it is well to seek and inquire.
A thousand paths wind through the mountain villages; every inch of time is an inch of gold.
In the midst of the great furnace and bellows of transformation, one turns the body about; when the mouth opens, one should know there is one who appreciates the sound.
How many monks stand side by side, tilting their ears, listening as his commands shake the entire forest.
In the same rhyme. Fisherman’s Retreat:
The river sky is vast and wide, my thoughts drift on. Fish and turtles float and sink, following the current.
Turning the prow toward the Eastern Sea, I shall not hesitate to re-bait my hook for the Great Turtle.
I sent the attendant Zhen and the Chan practitioner from Zhongling to Mount Ou. Entering my room, he sought instruction in the supreme school.
I intended to bestow upon him the true command, yet the staff by my bedside remains unopened.
Seeing off the Chan guest Kong:
his household livelihood is nothing at all; he scatters pearls like sand and grit. I, an old man, am so poor I have not even a single awl to rest upon;
yet with eyes upon my staff, I can distinguish dragons from snakes.

The mind at rest in the fast, all myriad conditions severed, forgetting self and others; Suddenly emptying the three periods of time, transcending names and forms. Outside the curtain of night-illumination, the clay ox bellows;
The waves of the ocean of awakening have dried up to their very depths.
I send Master Cuyang this "tortoise hair" to plant before his eyes; it provokes a full-cheeked smile from onlookers.
Should anyone ask about this matter hereafter, do not say you have come directly from Mount Jing.
Four Poems on the Mutual Reversal of Delusion and Enlightenment by Master Ximingiao Fine, drifting plum rain sprinkles the precarious heights;
Sitting alone in vast stillness, ten thousand anxieties clear away. The paths overgrown with weeds, human traces are few;
At the head of my bed, a single cane staff rests idly.
In the fifth month, the mountain cottage is as cold as ice; on the dusty marketplace, there is bustling clamor.
When the consciousness of profit and fame has entirely subsided, one is a monk beyond the mundane world, utterly serene and at ease.
Do not say that heaven and earth violate the Great Trust; the inner box and its lid are impartial, all in accord with nature.
The blue seas and mulberry fields change of their own accord, yet every dharma does not depart from the Mind-Ground Seal.

When the mind-ground is not yet clarified, it is a scorching heat; even when it is clarified, it remains as if it had never been. Cherish this and travel everywhere to visit the guests of the patriarchs;
thus you shall continue the true lamp for all time to come.
I send off Attendant Heng, who has served by my side for years. There is not a single word he can transmit or proclaim. He need not waste time copying on paper;
thirty strokes of the black staff are what he must face.
Sending off Abbot Suan:
three calls to receive the command, washing water with water; one silence to repay the monk, emptying emptiness.
Uprooting the long-standing nails and pegs, from the eight sides of the staff’s tip, a pure breeze arises.
As the Abbot Zheng opens the treasury of the True Canon, what is there that is not revealed? Head after head is entirely one's own treasure.
Having personally secured the ancestral deed, it is more than sufficient to benefit and deliver others.
In the same rhyme: Sending off Chan Master Xing back to Mount Zhongshan.
Perpetual activity dwells forever in the *nāga*-samādhi; To say it is "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is itself conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Go back to Mount Zhongshan and ask for the ultimate truth;
The old Chan master does not speak, only smiling faintly.
To layman Zhou Puming:
Reciting the Buddha’s name is nothing other than reciting one’s own mind. One’s own mind is the Buddha; do not seek it elsewhere.
The trees and groves before your eyes, along with the ponds and marshes, can still proclaim the sound of the Dharma day and night.
Two Verses on Hézé Tiānlín Residing at Zhìmén Ten years of roaming lakes and seas, fully satiated with inquiry and study;
I am well-accustomed to grasping the whisk made of tortoise hair.
On this day, having attained the seat and donned the robe, May you propagate the Dharma-gift throughout the southeast.
Baiyan sits in great stillness to test those who come to study; this authentic hammer demands that you take it up.
Though the monastic groves are filled with venerable elders, I do not know who can act as the compass needle.
Two Poems on Rhyme Composed of Self-Description:
When the Buddha came, he did not permit the monks to leave for their meal; even Deshan’s white staff was too weary to be raised.
Ashamed that I lack the functional pivot to deploy, I sit facing south, huddled in my room.
In my old age, I no longer attend the court audiences; the colored brushes I once held before the Emperor have long since been laid aside.
Having been graced by the King’s gift of a Daoist robe, an official of the Inner Court escorted me out through the south of the Wumen Gate.
To the lay devotee Hu Juejian, [the Master] showed that every person is the original, true Buddha within themselves. Day and night, throughout the six periods, they constantly radiate light.
If you can see this directly by raising your eyebrows, why labor to take a special journey to worship in the Western Paradise?
In the same rhyme, a reply to Chan Master Songyue, the true bone-descendant of the Abbot of Nanhu:
Nanhu sits firmly established; he should indeed be honored as the most venerable. Morning inquiries and evening requests abound with many fellow practitioners of Chan.
Each one, upon meeting the critical moment, has fully opened the crown of their head.

Master Yao, the Head Seat, returns from preaching the Dharma within the Tuṣita Palace. Under the blue sky and bright sun, the winds and thunder roll; how many remain stuck in their shells, lost in delusion?
Their extraordinary deliberations are covered in dust.
The first character of the scripture given to Chan Master Zhen no one recognizes; the annotations are in vain, for there are so many of them.
Who will take a three-foot-long blow-dry sword and, right before our eyes, cut through the tangle of vines?
To those fellow practitioners who wish to investigate the supreme pivot of the Chan school: don the armor of diligence and exert your full prowess;
with the sword of wisdom, tear asunder the net of ignorance, and you shall surely attain the "Pass with Honors" of the emptying of the mind.
I show you, Daoist Master Miaolian of Tang:
it is difficult to dwell long within this world of the five turbidities. When will this vast ocean of kalpas ever dry up?
If one can, in a single casual thought, empty the three periods of time, then such a person is called a "woman-warrior."
In ancient times, Shao played the *xun* flute for his attendant, performing the "Mysterious Sound of Great Commencement" nine times.
It was heard that auspicious phoenixes once danced in the court of Yu. For three thousand years, the golden strikes and jade responses have continued;
yet this is not easily heard unless one is a true connoisseur.

In the same rhyme: Sending off Attendant Jing— Before the bird’s nest even stirred, the down fell first. With mouth opened wide, it was clearly on that other side. How laughable—that his capacity for penetration was not subtle enough;
He lost his eyesight before the skull was even struck.
The attendant Sūnzàng has completed his study of Chan. Last night, empty space laughed heartily.
The luminous treasury inherent in every person is now opened with a jade key through a golden lock.
I present this record to the Secretary Zhong, who bears the burden of the Tathāgata’s Supreme Vehicle; he is also capable in the diverse teachings of the hundred schools.
Behold how the Secretary Yuan Foyin continued the fifth-generation lamp of Yunmen.
Auspicious bamboo shoots and divine sprouts first grow within the Jetavana Grove; in the end, they shall be seen reaching toward the heavens with flourishing branches.
It is not for the sake of manifesting the horns and head of a dragon-king, but so that the auspicious phoenix from the Crimson Mountain may come to grace us with its presence.
Master Zhen, the Abbot, has attained clear realization and employs it authentically; entering the gate, we meet face-to-face, his essence serene and profound.
Within the Tathāgatagarbha lies the mani jewel, yet viewed with the eyes of ordinary perception, it is but dust.

Ten Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains Deeply dwelling at the mountain peak, worldly thoughts are forgotten; There is no further Buddha-dharma to be deliberated upon. When the sun has risen fifteen feet high, I finally rise from sleep;
A single trellis of rosebushes is in full, fragrant bloom.
Sitting in a heap upon the stones at the roots of pines, a single cloud of leisure drifts away and returns. Few are the keen and intelligent monks who pass by;
for whom does the wooden gate remain open all day long?
Clouds and mountains fill the eyes; spring is silent and still. The peach and plum trees, wordless, are drenched in the midday sun.
When all activities cease directly beneath one, why labor further to point the Way?
The path enters the sheep-gut folds, grass brushing against the waist; A few thatched huts nestle beside the mountain peak. Only the moon at the edge of the sky understands my heart;
How many times has it flown down to accompany my solitude?
The incense seals have faded and the midday nap has ended; distant mountains enter the view, their blue layers upon layers. In this world of purity and peace, there is no constraint:
I am but a single monk who walks for long stretches, subsisting on gruel and rice.
Upon his body, coarse hair bristles beneath his patched robe; shaken out, the blue-grey dust flies through the window.
Before the gate, a small dog barks and howls, joyfully seeing the mountain boy returning with rice on his back.
I wander alone upon the empty steps after the rain. The autumn colors are somber and cool as the sun’s shadow sinks low. A single cry of a woodcutter comes from the mouth of the valley;
the bamboo pheasant flies up to the treetop and calls.
Living in the world, my heart is like ice in the twelfth month; dwelling in the mountains, I laugh at myself for being capable of nothing. Let us not fry oil to cook our vegetable soup;
let some be left to light the Buddha-lamp before the hall.

The stone chamber is vast and silent as I sit amidst the azure mists; friends and old associates from the rivers and lakes come and go but rarely. To the southeast, many "dragons and elephants" gather at the monastic seats;
I wonder who among them is singing the ancestral melody?
Dwelling in seclusion, I pass my years as circumstances allow; I bear the burden of my ancestral lineage, yet feel ashamed of having left the household life.
A wind that scrapes the earth rises through the night, and once more I behold the spring colors upon the plum blossoms.

Five Poems on Occasion in the Mountains on an Autumn Day Having finished my meal, I stroll through the mountains and pluck cassia branches; I have transplanted a secluded orchid to the edge of my steps. The green sprouts of vegetables grow within the garden;
White flat-bean flowers bloom across the entire fence.
Boiling vegetables without salt, too lazy to go out for more; the mendicant begging for alms has not yet returned home. Picking up this single hundred-patch robe to look at it:
last night the frost added flowers upon the roof-tiles.

In old age, I have come to cherish the forests and springs for my dwelling. With hands hanging down, what heart could I have to enter the world again? Let me try to dust off my pair of straw sandals at the foot of the bed;
when the weather clears, I shall move them out to dry before the eaves.
Yellow leaves flutter in the wind; the mountain cottage is cold and desolate all day long.
As the cook leans against the hearth, the young wood-gatherer arrives at evening, carrying wild pears on his shoulder.
The buckwheat flowers bloom as the morning sun shines clear; I call forth my young attendant to hear my instructions:
"Gather the purple yams well, and take your long spade to dig for *fuling* mushrooms."
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Seven;
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, Volume Eight.
Compiled by his disciples Daozhe and others.
Poem (Five-Syllable Octave):

A Sequel to the Four Songs of Master Guyuan on Mount Shansou Dwelling beside the deep clouds, my heart knows contentment within itself. The days are long through the vine-covered window; I idly read the Chan sutras.
