The desolate paths bear no traces of human presence; for sustenance, there are many wild herbs. Outside the gate, the spring grasses are green; deer and elk dwell here, their minds free from artifice.
The trees in the courtyard possess a fine beauty, and rare birds offer many melodious songs. It is a single, undifferentiated realm, where the mind is entirely devoid of discrimination.
In my leisure, I often sit alone; when a poem is finished, I recite it myself. Deep and remote is the path through the pines; far-reaching and vast is the depth of the white clouds.
The one who dwells in the mountain hermitage is originally a guest beyond the mundane world. When the autumn wind suddenly rises high, his grass robes shiver in the cold.
Quietly listening to the sound of flowing springs, sitting and watching pine seeds fall. Whence comes this cowherd boy, bare-shouldered with both feet exposed?
The tall forests are entirely stripped bare; the earth-scraping frost winds blow. The man of the Way does not leave the mountain; throughout the year he knows nothing.
When the single mind is empty and still, upon what shall the myriad dharmas rely? The bright moon rises over the gateway of the sea, its cool light shining upon the withered pine branches.

Presented to the Abbot Min: one who has seen the Way and is able to cultivate it; one who knows gratitude and ought to repay it. Great achievement is fundamentally without a master; the wondrous carving leaves no trace at all.
The treasury of spiritual powers in every land; the gate of wisdom-illumination in every atom. Before the impulse arises, the living eye is opened; with a single phrase, heaven and earth are settled.
Presented to the Layman Li Guming, who is able to study the Buddha while remaining at home:
he observes the precepts and vows to do so for his entire life. If you wish to realize the fruit of non-action (*asamskṛta*), you must eliminate the causes of outflows (*āsrava*).
Every instance is a perfect manifestation; each and every thing accords with true nature. Though dwelling within the realm of worldly toil, one may truly be called a person of liberation.
The Great Way of the Master Miaoxin has no fixed location;
it is fully realized in every single thing. As soon as deluded sentiments are suddenly stilled, the enlightened nature is spontaneously perfect and luminous.
An ancient mirror is polished until it shines; true gold is refined through a hundred smeltings. Behold the girl Lingzhao, whose virtuous fame resounds for a thousand years.

To the Chan practitioner Mi, who practices in seclusion and employs the secret: you must be one with the ancients. When principle is still, phenomena are also still; when the mind is empty, dharmas are likewise empty.
To explore the profound mysteries, one must possess the eye; to seek the Buddha in vain is to labor in obscurity. My true teaching is vividly present within the grandeur of daily life.

Sent by Tianxi En, this guest master’s instruction on contemplation and Chan is fundamentally beyond agreement or difference. Heart-mind after heart-mind, there is no grasping or rejecting; phenomenon after phenomenon, they naturally interpenetrate.
Ultimate reality is originally not a form; true emptiness is likewise not empty. Held lightly upon a crystal platter, it suddenly reveals the family style.
To the layman Shi Ye:
among those who study the Buddha while remaining at home throughout ancient and modern times, how many truly know? Once you have awakened to the original mind, why must you abandon wife and children?
Pang Daoyuan of Xiangxi and Pei Gongmei of Hedong spread their witty sayings throughout the Zen groves, and their fragrant names are recorded in the monastic histories.
To Layman Shiweng:

Your original nature is the true Buddha; majestic within the midst of daily life, you have already diligently cultivated the resolve for the Way—you should now advance in the practice of seated meditation.
Wherever one touches, there is no obstruction; when the moment arrives, there is flexibility and adaptability. If the mind is empty, one can attain the highest rank;
thus, one may be the equal of the old Pang.
At the summit of Yunju, the site has long been overgrown and desolate. I, having taken charge as abbot, resolved to restore it. Thereupon, I personally...

Cao took up baskets and spades and was the first to construct dwellings there to reside in. However, as the times were difficult and his great undertaking remained unfulfilled, he felt that these magnificent forests and springs were a fitting place to conceal his inadequacies.
As sights before him evoked his reflections, he composed ten verses to show to those around him, saying: [The ten verses follow.]

At the summit, where the clouds are deep, lies the site of Master Ying’s former hermitage. Since it has passed through the conflagration at the end of an eon, one perceives that times have become perilous.

Grass has swallowed the stupa nestled in the rock crevices; vines entwine the stone stele lying by the path. Now that the wilderness is cleared during this sagely age, one delights in the non-action of Chan recitation.
At the summit where the clouds are deep, who can discuss one’s life? Pulling at bracken to mend the roof is difficult; planting trees side-by-side easily forms a gate.

Dust gathers especially thick upon the damp desk; the fire in the hearth remains though the embers are cold. A single cry of a mountain pheasant resounds; before one knows it, dusk has fallen once more.
Deep within the clouds at the mountain’s summit, I now vow to take up residence. Though I till the weeds until they can no longer grow, there remains no surplus of wild ferns and bracken to eat.
The ancient stone steps have long since crumbled; this empty hall is but newly constructed. There must surely be a destined sequence for decline and prosperity—what, then, is the will of Heaven?
At the summit where the clouds are deep, the myriad peaks stand ranged like screens. In the wind-swept forest, spring rustles; the misty trees at dawn are dark and dim.
I have sharpened the handle of my blunt hoe and begun to whet the long sickle. Having already formed my plan for reclusion, I build a garden beside my thatched gate.
At the summit where the clouds are deep, who can accompany one in this solitude? If these green mountains were wearisome, even the bright days would be hard to endure.
Gathering herbs, I ascend rocky caves; gazing at pines, I lean against stone bridges. I am ashamed of my own worthless and scattered nature, unable to contribute to this Sage and Bright Age.
At the summit, where the clouds are deep, my summer retreat satisfies my simple heart. The red dust of the world cannot fly here;

the green trees naturally form their own shade. Fine birds sing before the door; extraordinary flowers bloom throughout the forest. A guest arrives from beyond the mundane world, trailing his staff by the edge of the emerald stream.
At the summit where the clouds are deep, who can converse of this school? Alone I clear the weeds at the steps, idly caressing the pines by the rocks.

Cold and heat are met with the three-fold robe; heaven and earth are measured by the seven-foot staff. The hall is entered as the wild rice porridge is cooked; the novice boy strikes the bell just then.
At the summit, where the clouds are deep, the meditation hall is more still and secluded. Monkeys cry out under the clear night moon; wild geese pass through the azure autumn sky.
Frost-covered fruits, fragrant and ready for plucking; cold cypress trees, their emerald hue seeming to flow. From of old, human tracks have been few; what need is there to cease social visits?
At the summit where the clouds are deep, what has been my life’s pursuit for so many years? With a single mind free from attachment, all myriad thoughts have been utterly consumed.
I rejoice in having few social encounters; who would say that solitude is excessive? Having yellow tubers to satisfy hunger, why would I descend again into the misty vines?
At the summit, where the clouds are deep, no brush and ink can capture it. The light of the stream is even more beautiful in the clear weather; the flow of the spring is especially pure at night.
If one can but find the delight within the mountains, why strive for fame in the world? In the small window, the cold moon is white; a single branch of plum blossoms stretches across.

In praising Avalokiteśvara, he opens the gate of perfect penetration; manifesting in the form of a bhikṣu, his wondrous responses are boundless and his true compassion immeasurable. His entire being is surrendered—
Within the thicket of grass, only Sudhana was able to draw near;

holding the Cintāmaṇicakra in his hand, he gazed upward at the moon in the heavens. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands wide open, where all that has been taught throughout the three periods of time is revealed.
Guanyin with the Fish Basket:

The glistening scales are fresh and brimming with vitality. Held aloft in her bare hands, she wanders through the dust of the marketplace. Noble and base alike, there is no fixed price according to the season;
those who encounter her are not merely passing travelers.
The Cloth Bag Monk drags his bag across the marketplace; whenever he meets someone, he asks for a single coin.
He knows only how to chase after children’s games, forgetting the Tuṣita Heaven above.
The morning sun mends the tattered robe with earnest needling and pricking;
the effort must be continuous and meticulous. If this time it cannot be mended, one will have brought shame upon the sun at the edge of the sky.
Facing the moon, I finish the remaining sutra.
A single scroll of scripture in hand; a single orb of moon in the sky. Clearly manifest before one’s eyes, who can it be said to explain it so plainly?

A host of Arhats worthy of offerings—what a bunch of blockheads! What have they been doing all these years? Though their supernatural powers may manifest transformations, they lack the transmission and upholding of the Buddha-Dharma.
I wish to examine my own transgressions; I have not yet been spared the pricking of needles and awls. When will this grasping at the strange ever end? Who can truly describe it?
For a long time I dwelt in the stillness of Tiantai, seeking a secluded retreat. What urgent business has brought you out of the mountains?
You know only how to cross the sea to seek alms, unaware that from long ago your face has been covered in dust.
The Arhat Ox-Crosser holds a scripture in his hand while astride a rhinoceros. Knowing who this old bhikṣu has come as, he simply follows the fragrant grasses away.
Upon returning home, one ought to have turned back long ago.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma has a missing tooth in his front row and thick eyebrows; he is this single-transmission blue-eyed barbarian.
His utterances did not accord with the Son of Heaven, and his crossing of the river was in vain for a stalk of reed.

The Sixth Patriarch, our distant ancestor, came from afar to this eastern land as the First Patriarch. Outside the Teaching, how could there ever have been a separate transmission? Sitting coldly for nine years, he reached no resolution;
carrying his single sandal alone, he returned to the Western Heaven.
Searching for the mind, one finds it not; the peace of mind is thus settled. Suddenly, half of the nostrils are lost. Rising after three prostrations, he stands in his place.
The robe and bowl of Shaolin were transmitted by him.
Within Mount Huánggōng, he alone conceals his radiance; his reputation and traces are entirely forgotten by the world.
He entices a śrāmaṇera to come and inquire about the Dharma, yet from beginning to end, they remain fundamentally at odds.
Three times he firmly declined the Emperor’s decree; for his entire life, he ought to have dwelt only within the mountains.
How is it that he still had the leisure of mind to ascend directly to Niutou to receive Lanrong?
This is merely the seven-year-old son of the Zhou family; who else has known his past fabrications? He knows how to speak of a surname that is no ordinary surname;
clearly, there is still one more nail missing from the back of his head.
Enlightenment is not a tree; the mirror is not a stand. Opening one's mouth, how could one know it is a source of calamity? Having transmitted the robe and bowl, what use would they be?
At the third watch under the moon, he departed from Huangmei.
Chan Master Lanzan wore coarse cloth with knotted seams and his hair was streaked with gray. Though the Son of Heaven summoned him, he would not descend from the mountain.
He incurred a hollow reputation that has endured for generations, simply because he shared his yams with a layman.
The Sleeping Tiger at Old Master Huqiu is a sight the world admires; yet anyone who dares to touch the massed clouds becomes his enemy.
He must surely be intoxicated by flesh within the empty mountains, never again baring his claws and fangs before men.

In the *Three Laughs* painting, the Son of Heaven summoned them, yet they would not leave the mountains; when seeing off a guest, they even crossed the Tiger Creek bend. One truly knows that Tao and Lu were no ordinary men;
their refined elegance for a thousand ages lies within a single laugh.
Master Gaofeng established the "Deadly Barrier" on Mount Tianmu; from this, the *huatou* descended into the human world.
Beneath the green pines upon the Pan-tuo rocks, his austere and lofty spirit—who could possibly emulate it?

Master Zhongfeng, who dwelt in the Huanzhu Hermitage, was an old master of the school whose eye atop his head was perfectly upright for discerning dragons from snakes. Observe how he opened his mouth to benefit others:
he would chew up empty space and swallow it whole without spitting it out.
Master Qianyan, the Old Man of Wuming on Mount Fulong—
once he was caught in the trap at Lion Rock, his "confession" was both dead and alive, yet still as formidable as a towering star.
To this day, he stirs wind and thunder from level ground.
Master Taesong (invited by Elder Pu-gyeong Jin):
Having traveled early through the gates of all quarters, he never followed conventional paths; he raised his stiff backbone—a single bolt of raw iron.
Arriving at Mount Zituo, one meets a tumble upon level ground; both eyes are knocked out. To whom can this grievance be entrusted for redress?
At Yandang, cold clouds are swept away; in Longyuan, the bright moon is played with. In both places, firm barriers are established; the application of the pivot differs from that given to others.
His majestic presence was awe-inspiring, shaking the entire monastic community. Master Shizi taught his cubs the secret method for guiding them.
Elder Huì of Tàipíng invited Gu Dìng Wǔshàng to don the armor of patience and raise the banner of diligence.
Without establishing the three barriers, the hordes of demons were naturally subdued. His virtue was honored and his station was eminent.

His principle excelled and his words were vast. In his later years, he resided at Jingwu, where his fame spread to foreign lands. He revealed the seal of the wondrously luminous mind-ground, turning the flow of the Eastern Sea back into the Western River.
Master Zhigan possessed a single-handled axe that was his very person;
he sat upon the site of enlightenment six times, and his Way was transmitted through both the orthodox and collateral lines, his fame shaking all quarters.

He launched the boat of compassion to briefly roam the Lize marshes, and suspended the sun of wisdom for a long stay in Qiantang. There, the dragon of Longyuan leaped forth, and the phoenix of Fengtai soared high.
Soaring aloft, he has already laid bare his sincerity and expounded the Great Teaching; ever more, he extends his hand to rectify the collapsing order of the Dharma.

Though his entire body remains unmanifest, there is nowhere in the universe where it cannot be concealed. Within a single hair-tip, hundreds of thousands of samādhis appear; throughout the forests of the four seas, the discourse grows ever more profound.
Master Songyin (who was Wuyan): his character was as firm as pine and bamboo;
his spirit was as pure as jade and snow. His virtue was honored by the monastic community, and his reputation was esteemed by the civil elite.

His great function was fully manifested, like the moon reflected in a clear pool; his true mechanism responded universally, like the spring returning to withered trees. His equal compassion reached all things, manifesting everywhere.
In receiving people, he cast an iron net before Lion Rock; on the banks of the Huating River, he captured a qilin.

Master Jueyuan’s divine mechanisms were vast and open, his wise eloquence was like a surging torrent. He swallowed the Buddhas and patriarchs in his breath; his gaze fixed upon the clouds and the sky. He stirred the winds of transformation.
For a thousand *li*, his reputation has spread through two reigns; his lineage is transmitted without error, and his conduct is worthy of praise.
This caused Wang Fuzhong to prostrate and submit with heartfelt admiration, much like Masui before Pángjù and Yàoshān before Lǐáo.
Alas! That the gate of Jièshì relies upon this elder means that the Dharma-way of Xīqiū has not yet fallen into profound desolation.
In self-praise: my face is colder than iron; my heart is as dead as ashes. There is no Zen to speak of, and though I have a mouth, it is too weary to open.
Before the Hall of Heavenly Reception, I once sat at the imperial summons; atop Mount Lingxiao, I arrived immediately upon receiving the decree. Limping and dragging along, I am a fool.
Dull and stupid! A blind shaveling who brings calamity to the monastic groves. With his old fists, he seeks to strike the cheeks of Zen practitioners.
This Elder Zhuzhu of Longtan was originally a monk from Zhejiang;
having come to serve as a guest in Jiangxi, he opens his mouth to revile others, making it difficult for him to set foot anywhere.
A broken sand pot cannot be lifted; iron sorrel paste is but a vain chewing. Sitting alone on the peak of Mount Ou, how cold and desolate is the gateway!
A net of tortoise hair spread in hundreds of thousands of layers—intended to strike the golden pheasant in the heavens.

The Elder Chan’an Can was like a wooden ladle for a head and a bronze bell for eyes; he was seldom loved by people and often hated by them. He did not practice Zen, yet he insisted on raising public cases (*gong'an*);
he could not read a single character, yet he claimed to understand the sutras. He cut off the orthodox lineage of Songyuan and extinguished the flame of Jie.
The true lamp of the chamber; for people there is no standard, and in the monastery there are no rules or ropes. Atop a thousand peaks, one roams freely;
throughout the ten-thousand-li universe, there is but a single monk in his patchwork robe.

The Elder Tonglingde has no virtue worthy of praise and lacks any talent worth taking up. Seated upon the lion throne, he brandishes his fly-whisk with careless ease; his appearance resembles that of a monk, yet his speech is devoid of any principle.
He acts like one driven by wind and madness, shifting between anger and joy at whim, and even picks up fresh reeds and brooms [to play with].
Sweeping away the clouds over Mount Ou, he overturned the sand basin;

drawing up all the waters of the Dragon Abyss, those who know him say his fundamental capacity is more than sufficient, while those who do not know him say his fabrications are beyond compare. Sometimes west, sometimes east;
suddenly there, suddenly here. With feet treading the golden boat, the sea moon is high; on the Poyang Lake, a pure breeze arises.

The Elder Tianlongshan requested that he speak on the essential teaching of his life: the Zen of the blind. How can one dig into the earth to find the heavens? Dwelling in the mountains in these three places, my poverty has pierced to the bone;
I have no robes or bowl to pass on to others.
Riding upon the treasury of the Tripitaka by imperial decree, I receive the grace of the Golden Palace and serve the majesty of Heaven. Atop the Five-Tufted Peak, I chant the ancestral pivot.
In my old age, I am so poor that I have not even a single awl to stand upon; I rub my two eyes and watch the clouds fly.
The late Master Wuzhun of Bafa,
an elder who transmitted the lineage and preached the Dharma, engaged in the samādhi of playful artistry through poetry and calligraphy during his leisure from these activities.
Therefore, even a single phrase or solitary character that has drifted down into the human world is, for those who obtain it, no less than the *sui-zhu* pearl or the *bian-bi* jade.
Now, the attendant Shan-shi has treasured this true manuscript and brought it forth to show me, requesting that I write words upon its back. I therefore said to him:
"When the conversation reaches the end of the night and the mountain moon emerges, one again rides a white deer into the deep clouds; take care not to treat this as [merely] a painting."
Poetic Assembly. You are the direct descendant; if you wish to see the workings of this old man, you must further raise your eyes high before you can succeed.
Postscript by Monk Zhongfeng’s calligraphic manuscript.
The Elder Huanzhu’s dharma-nature is vast and his waves are wide; he speaks with abandon and writes as his brush moves.
Every word reveals that extraordinary and momentous matter prior to the existence of both sentient beings and Buddhas.

Now, observing the Dharma discourse he bestowed upon Lady Atalun, he employs unimpeded eloquence to elucidate the profound meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*; it may truly be said that he has pierced through Śākyamuni.
Although this is so regarding the nostrils of Laozi, from the perspective of the gate of the patch-robed monks (samneng), it still lacks final decisiveness.
Master Wuzang, treasure these remaining calligraphic traces. Furthermore, tell me: what is the ultimate intent behind my making such a statement?
The Monk Mingwen of the Doushuai Garden in Wumen read this. The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhuang of A’an (End).
Epitaph (with Preface):
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month, the *guīyǒu* day, in the first year of the Yongle era of the Great Ming, at my Jingshan...
The sixtieth incumbent, Chan Master Daiman Zhuang, manifested illness and passed away in his private quarters at Budong Xuan (Hall of Immovability).
His worldly age was fifty-eight, and his monastic seniority was forty-five.

His disciples, including Tandan and others, were able to follow his final instructions, performing the rites from the enshrouding and burial through the cremation and interment without any deviation from the prescribed protocols. In the following year...
I subsequently assumed the leadership of the temple. At the outset of my administration, I observed that its established regulations were orderly and the monastic community was harmonious;
whatever was undertaken was systematic and free from confusion. Arranged in east-west rows, each official performed his respective duty.

Reflecting upon my own declining age and infirmity as I occupied this position by default, I have simply followed the old precedents; like Xiao He’s rules followed by Cao Can, I have maintained them with the utmost diligence.
Shortly thereafter, as the stele for the Master’s stupa remained uninscribed, his disciples compiled a record of his life and deeds and requested that I compose the inscription.
Finding it improper to decline on principle, I have consulted the record and extracted its main points, setting them down here in straightforward prose. The Chan Master’s name was Puzhuang;
his courtesy name was Jingzhong; "Aiman" (Dumb Hermit) was his alternative appellation. His lineage was the Yuan clan of Xianju in Tiantai, a family whose ancestral succession...
Regarding his Confucian studies: His mother was Lady Wang. On the evening of the Master’s birth, she dreamed that a Buddhist monk entered her room.

He was born on the twelfth day of the eighth month of the seventh year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the Bingxu year. At one year of age, he was precocious and exceptionally gifted, unlike ordinary children.
Shanben had cultivated these roots from an early age and had long since renounced the consumption of pungent vegetables. At the age of eight, he carried his book-satchel to enter the local school;
when taught the Odes and the Documents, he could recite them upon hearing them once. He always loved solitude and quietude, sitting upright as if lost in thought.

As if speaking in a dream, he would admonish himself, saying: "To read books and clarify principles is the way of living in this world. To study the Dharma that transcends the world is truly my aspiration. At the age of twelve, he addressed [his parents].
His parents sought to have him renounce the household life; though they cherished him dearly, in the end none could thwart his resolve.

It happened that a paternal uncle of his clan, who had followed the Śākya teachings, returned home. He was subsequently taken by him to Ningbo. There, Chan Master Lian of Zu’ān resided at Tiantong, where the Dharma seat was very flourishing.
Upon seeing [the boy], the Master took him under his care. The following year, Jihai (1579), he shaved his head and received full ordination. He donned—
Lao attended as a servant for a long time, yet they did not reach a point of mutual resonance. He took his leave and traveled to Tianning Monastery in the prefectural city.

At that time, Master Liaotang Yi was raising the koan of the broken sandpot to examine the capacities of those who came to him. The Master went straight to the abbot’s quarters. Liaotang asked, “Where have you come from?”

The attendant replied, "A celestial youth. Xuedou said, "Braving the rain and piercing the cold, what such desperate urgency is this? The attendant replied, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent.
Xuedou asked, "What is the matter of birth and death? The master made a striking motion with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).
Xuedou said, "You dare to pluck the tiger’s whiskers here! "Go to the meditation hall," he added. One day, in the hall, Xuedou brought up the cypress tree in front of the courtyard.

Regarding the story of Shuzi: As the Master was about to open his mouth, Tang struck him across the face with his palm. Shuzi attained sudden enlightenment and was subsequently admitted into the inner quarters.

There, he engaged in daily investigation and discernment until he reached the ultimate depths of the teaching. Before long, he returned to visit Zu’an, who, observing that his spiritual acuity was extraordinary, ordered him to take charge of the treasury keys.
Not long after, Tang moved his banner to Tiantong; the Master’s joy was manifest in both his voice and countenance.
Master Sè applied himself with even greater diligence.

In the *ding-si* year of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued ordering the monastics throughout the empire to study and lecture upon the three sutras: the *Heart Sutra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Master Minggong, the Abbot of Jinshan in Zhenjiang, invited the Master to provide instruction and inspire his disciples, analyzing and elucidating the scriptures.

His meaning was profoundly in accord with the principles of the occasion, and the audience was deeply convinced and submissive; his reputation grew exceedingly great. The following year, Wumou (1398), he stayed as a guest at Tien-chieh Monastery.
There were two great elders there, Chuan-shih and Man-an, whose status and reputation were highly esteemed, yet whom the Master could rival.

They engaged him in debate on various occasions, exhausting the depths of the fundamental treasury [of the Dharma], and they praised him without end, considering that he had personally grasped the very marrow of their late master. At the point of death...
The True Lineage of Deliverance truly has its entrusted purpose. The following year, the Year of Jihwei (1279), he was invited to take charge of the world at Beichan in Fuzhou.
On the day he opened the hall, he burned incense as an offering of gratitude to Liangtao; beneath his sweeping gesture, the obscured was revealed and the ignorant were enlightened.

Monks and laypeople alike turned toward him in devotion. He lamented that this ancient temple had dilapidated buildings and a depleted community of monks, and thus, with an urgency for practical achievement, he began its restoration.

He restored what had fallen into ruin. The halls, shrines, corridors, and eaves, along with the bells and fish-shaped chimes, were rebuilt, plastered, and decorated; everything was renewed. He then moved his residence to Yunju.
Previously, as the temple had been abandoned for a long time, its name remained while its reality had vanished. On the day the Master assumed the abbacy, [the community gathered].

He vowed at the old site to bind straw together and gather a multitude, plotting the restoration of the temple. When the elder Quanshi heard of this, he marveled, saying, "Truly, you are a mountain-dweller of the true essence.
He resided there for barely five years; through soliciting donations and managing the construction, he labored among the many craftsmen until the temple buildings were completed.

There, the great sea-monsters roared and thundered, and the golden and azure structures soared like soaring pheasants. Thus, the profound mysteries of the Dharma were extensively propagated throughout Jiangyou.
Walking alone, in the spring of the twenty-sixth year, the year of Guiyou (1093),

an imperial edict was issued to summon eminent śramaṇas of high conduct from throughout the realm; the Master was selected as the foremost candidate, and his public presentation of his views pleased the Emperor,
fully satisfying His Majesty’s expectations.

In the autumn of this year, the Emperor’s decree arrived, ordering the performance of sacrifices and the erection of a stele at Mount Lu. The holy spirit was moved and responded, manifesting auspicious omens and radiating light; divine lamps shone forth in reflection.
Auspicious mists swirled and gathered; from the top to the bottom of the stele altar, they dazzled the eyes of the multitudes.
The officials, monks, Daoists, and commoners attending the sacrifice prostrated themselves in refuge and praised him with one voice.
When the rites were completed and he returned to his post, the Emperor’s brows moved in joy. He was granted a full set of robes, a mark of exceptional honor. That winter, he obtained...
The Imperial Decree stated: "Sheng shall reside at Mount Jing. This temple is the foremost monastery of the Chan school within the realm;

we appoint you, Master, to dwell therein, so as to bring the highest honor to the Way of the Teacher. Once the Master arrived, he cultivated the foundations of the Teaching and expanded the source of the Way.
He continued the radiant flame of former luminaries and provided a ladder for those who follow. On the walls of the hall appeared the manifestation of Avalokiteśvara from the Sea of Rocks.
The temple bell modeled after the great instruments of the Fu clan was cast; the hermitage at Mount Zhongfeng was established, revealing that the ancestral lamp had a successor.

Fields were distributed to tenant farmers to exempt them from the collection of official rents. Prince Daohuai bestowed the gift of a brocade-wrapped *samghāṭī* robe, manifesting the karmic opportunity of "untying his sash to leave behind his robes.
Renowned officials offered their full support, the three schools yielded in virtue, and the fourfold assembly settled their minds therein.

His station was honored throughout his lifetime; it can truly be said that his mastery was exhaustive. Alas! The teaching is in peril during this age of decline, and the Way has lost its great masters.
His final words were left unfulfilled as he suddenly passed into stillness. Seven days later, his body was cremated; wherever the smoke and flames reached—
The śarīra [relics] shone brilliantly; his *mālā* [rosary], amidst the ashes and embers, remained unbroken.
His remains were enshrined in a stupa upon the southern slope of Mount Xiaoxiao. His disciples and followers, their grief profound, faced one another in sorrowful lamentation.
Some spoke among the assembly, saying: "The Master entered the Great Samādhi; we disciples can only gaze upon him with longing and admiration through this stūpa alone.
There were so-and-so many first-time disciples and so-and-so many disciples who attained the Dharma.
His recorded teachings from the three assemblies amount to so-and-so many fascicles, all of which have been transmitted. Yet, no inscription has been carved upon stone to commemorate them."
How may this be manifested for eternity? Thereupon, he requested an inscription. The inscription reads:
Majestic is Mount Tiantai, Above corresponding to the constellations; Vast and expansive, it gathers the vital energy of the earth, Concentrating wonders and manifesting excellence.
It gave birth to a great man, A leader of the Zen groves, Who assisted the world and supported the people, Providing secret protection to the state and its kin.
Liaotang Shuzhong and Tongdai Tachou—difficult brothers and difficult elder brothers—sang and played in alternation, masters of their school at the end of the Yuan dynasty.

Their virtue and conduct were truly flourishing. It was Master Dameng who, while still young and already soaring like a crane, encountered his teacher through long-standing karmic affinities in Gumo (Ningbo).
Under Taibai Tianning, he received the secret transmission of the mind-dharma.

He rectified the community in the Western River region; the circumstances of the time were as interlocking spokes. Wherever he went, his achievements were great, and he restored grand regulations to their former state.

He was rigorous and austere in self-discipline, and his instruction of disciples was characterized by skillful guidance. His reputation grew daily more eminent, spreading far and wide throughout the land.

When the Emperor issued an edict summoning eminent monks, he stood out preeminent among them. In responding to the imperial inquiry, he struck the essential point with perfect timing, and the honors bestowed upon him were most generous.
When his life was spent at Mount Jing, it was as if ascending Vulture Peak; the rain of Dharma fell in torrents, moistening and nourishing all beings.
Suddenly, during the day, he beheld a transformation: his power of expedient means having ceased, his body collapsed upon the twin peaks of the Double Path.
Monkeys howled and langurs leaped; amidst the chaos, how could a single piece of wood suffice?
Alas, the wise man—[inscriptions] at the corner of the stone hall.
